course.title: Astronomy: From Sky to Cosmos
course.description: Track the turning sky, weigh a planet, take a star's temperature and time the expanding universe, with real numbers throughout.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with algebra, powers of ten and ratios. Physics: Motion and Forces helps but is not required.

paragraphs: Astronomy is the study of the Sun, the Moon, the planets, the stars and the galaxies beyond them. People first took it up to keep calendars and to find their way across the sea, and they still pursue it to learn what the universe is made of and how old it is.

This course starts with what you can see from your own garden. The stars wheel round the sky through the night, and the Sun climbs higher in summer than in winter, and a little geometry explains both. The Moon’s phases and eclipses finish that first module. The course then moves outward, to orbits and gravity, then to starlight and what it says about a star’s temperature, distance and motion, and last to how stars live and die and how the universe began.
Every lesson works with real numbers, and you check each result for yourself.
outcomes: You’ll be able to predict how high the Sun or a star climbs from where you live, and which stars never set.
You’ll be able to explain the seasons, the phases of the Moon and why eclipses are rare.
You’ll be able to work out how long a planet takes to orbit the Sun and how fast a spacecraft must go to escape a planet.
You’ll be able to read a star’s temperature, distance and speed from its light.
You’ll be able to use the motion of distant galaxies to estimate the age of the universe.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with algebra, ratios and powers of ten, though no astronomy is assumed.

lessons.title: The turning sky

steps.headline: The sky turns because Earth does

lead.text: The cause is closer to home than the stars. Earth spins once a day, and you spin with it. Because you share the motion you don’t feel it, just as you don’t feel a train gliding along a smooth, straight track. What you notice is the world outside sliding the other way. From a train window the trees slide backwards while the train carries you forwards.
The sky does the same thing. Earth carries you round, and the stars seem to rise in the east, climb and set in the west. One full turn is 360 degrees, and Earth takes about 24 hours to make it.

Picture Earth from high above the North Pole, with you standing on the equator. Draw a dashed line from you to one distant star. It keeps the same direction no matter how far Earth turns, because the star is so remote that moving round Earth’s rim makes no visible difference to where it lies.

afterFigure.text: Follow the star from your point of view. It begins just above the horizon and climbs until it passes straight overhead, then sinks towards the opposite horizon. At last Earth’s own bulk comes between you and the star, and it has set. It stays hidden for about twelve hours before you are carried round far enough to see it rise again.

lead.text: Earth’s spin is steady, so the sky turns at the same rate all night.

reveal.text: Stars come back to the same place after 23 h 56 min, not 24 h, so a star rises about four minutes earlier each night. 24 hours is accurate enough for a night’s observing.

lead.text: That turning has a centre. Every wheel turns about an axle, and the sky’s axle is Earth’s own axis, the line that runs through the North Pole and the South Pole. Extend that line far out into space and it meets the sky at two spots, the north celestial pole and the south celestial pole.

Earth’s axis keeps pointing the same way through the night, so those two spots stay where they are while everything else turns around them. A turntable gives the picture: the spindle in the middle stays put while the record spins around it. From the northern hemisphere you can see the north celestial pole, and it is the hub of the wheel you watched on the first screen.

afterFigure.text: A star sits almost exactly on the north celestial pole. Polaris, the North Star, lies within a degree of it, so it barely moves all night, and people have used it for centuries to find north. It is often assumed to be the brightest star in the sky. It is only moderately bright, and its use comes from where it sits.
One more name before moving on. The point straight above your head is the zenith. It is a different spot from the celestial pole, and as Earth turns it slides across the stars.

lead.text: The last screen named two different spots in the sky: the hub of the wheel and the point overhead.
The next few screens work on one puzzle. The north celestial pole is a fixed spot among the stars, yet its height above your horizon depends on where on Earth you stand.

Suppose you start on the equator on a clear night and look north. The pole sits right on the horizon, so low that a hill or a row of trees would hide it. Now start walking north. With every day’s travel the pole stands a little higher. Keep going, and when you reach the North Pole itself you look up and find it straight overhead, with the whole sky wheeling around the spot above your head.

afterFigure.text: Somewhere between those two places is your own, and the pole stands at some height there. To work out that height we need two ways of measuring: one for how far north you have walked, and one for how high up in the sky something is. The next screen supplies them.

lead.text: The first measure is latitude. It is the angle, taken at Earth’s centre, between the equator and the line out to where you stand. The equator is at 0°, the North Pole is at 90° N, and Amsterdam, which this lesson uses as its example, is at about 52° N. Astronomers write latitude as φ, the Greek letter phi.
A degree of latitude is about 111 km of ground, so the walk from the equator to Amsterdam is roughly 5,800 km.

The second measure is altitude, the angle between the horizon and whatever you are looking at. Something sitting on the horizon has an altitude of 0°. Something straight overhead, at the zenith, has an altitude of 90°. Everything else falls in between.

Because altitude is an angle, it says nothing about distance. A star and an aircraft in the same direction have the same altitude. You can estimate it with your own hand: held at arm’s length, a fist covers about 10° of sky, so a star two fists above the horizon is at roughly 20°.

afterFigure.text: Now the walk can be put into numbers. On the equator, at latitude 0°, the north celestial pole stands at altitude 0°. At the North Pole, at latitude 90°, it stands at altitude 90°. What remains is everything in between.

lead.text: Along the walk north, the pole’s altitude rises steadily from 0° to 90°, just as the latitude does.

reveal.text: Whether you reasoned from the two ends of the walk or already knew the rule, the pole stands as many degrees up as your latitude. The next screen shows why.

steps.headline: The pole stands as high as your latitude

lead.text: The numbers matched, and a slice through Earth along its axis shows why. Draw it as you read: a circle for Earth with the axis as a vertical line through it, and a dot on the edge for you. You stand on the surface at latitude φ. Draw a line from Earth’s centre to your feet and it makes an angle φ with the equator. That is what latitude means.

Now think about your horizon. It is the flat line you see at your feet, where the ground meets the sky. It touches Earth at the spot where you stand and meets the line to Earth’s centre at a right angle. The arrow pointing straight up from your head is that same line carried outwards.

The pole is the last piece. It is so far away that it lies in the same direction from every place on Earth, parallel to the axis. Wherever you stand, you find it by looking along an arrow parallel to the axis. Call that the pole arrow and draw it from your dot.

afterFigure.text: Now compare angles. The line to Earth’s centre is 90° − φ from the axis, and your horizon is 90° from that line, so the angle between your horizon and the pole arrow is 90° − (90° − φ) = φ. That angle is the pole’s altitude. In the northern hemisphere the pole stands as many degrees above your horizon as your latitude, wherever you walk. Redraw your sketch at another latitude and the same result appears.

lead.text: For centuries sailors relied on exactly this fact. With a simple instrument for measuring angles and a clear night, a navigator could read the ship’s latitude from the height of the pole star.

steps.headline: Declination, and the size of a star’s circle

lead.text: So far we have followed the hub of the wheel. The stars that circle it need an address too, and astronomers borrow the idea from the map. Extend Earth’s equator out into space and you get the celestial equator, a circle in the sky halfway between the two celestial poles.

Declination, written δ (delta), is a star’s latitude on that sky: the angle between the celestial equator and the star, measured at Earth’s centre. A star on the celestial equator has declination 0°. A star at the north celestial pole has +90°, and one at the south celestial pole −90°. Stars north of the celestial equator carry a plus sign and stars south of it a minus sign.

A star keeps the same declination as Earth turns, which makes it a dependable address. The first three pictures show how declination is measured, and the last two show the circles that stars at different declinations trace round the pole.

afterFigure.text: Declination also tells you how big a star’s circle is. A star at declination δ lies 90° − δ from the north celestial pole, and as Earth turns it carries the star round the sky in a circle about the pole with exactly that radius.

Compare two stars. A star at declination +70° is 20° from the pole and traces a small circle. A star at declination 0° is 90° from the pole and traces the largest circle of all. Both complete their circle in the same 24 hours, so the second star has much further to travel and moves faster across the sky, the way a child at the edge of a roundabout covers more ground than one near the middle.

lead.text: A star’s declination says how far it lies north or south of the celestial equator.

Go back to your place on the walk, at latitude φ, where the pole stands φ above your horizon. Follow one star as it circles the pole. The lowest point of its circle lies directly below the pole, a distance 90° − δ lower, so the star’s lowest altitude is φ − (90° − δ). Use the buttons to compare three stars. The marker on each circle shows its lowest point and turns green when that point clears the horizon.

afterFigure.text: Whether the star ever sets depends on the sign of that number. If the lowest point is above 0°, the whole circle clears the horizon and the star stays in the sky all night, every night of the year. Astronomers call a star like that circumpolar, meaning “around the pole”. Setting φ − (90° − δ) greater than 0° and rearranging gives δ > 90° − φ. At latitude 60° N, for example, every star north of declination +30° is circumpolar. The further north you walk, the lower that limit falls, until by the North Pole it has reached 0°.

blocks.text: Go outside on a clear night, away from street lights. Give your eyes ten minutes to adjust. At first the sky looks still, a scatter of points pinned in place. Now pick one star above a rooftop or a tree and watch it for an hour. It has crept along a smooth arc, and so has every other star in the sky.

Face north and the pattern becomes clear. The arcs all curve around one spot, the way the grooves of a record curve around the spindle. Stars close to that spot sweep out small circles and stars further away sweep out big ones, and the circles never cross. The northern sky behaves like a wheel turning slowly about a hub.

That wheel is what this lesson is about. It starts with why the sky turns and what sits at the hub. It ends with a trick sailors used for centuries, reading how far north a ship has sailed from the height of that hub.

recap.nextHook: The stars keep their places in the turning sky, but the Sun does not: its height at noon changes through the year. The next lesson follows the shadow of a stick in a garden to find out why.

lessons.title: Why the seasons change

steps.headline: A tilted axis and a year-long orbit

lead.text: Two facts about Earth explain the changing shadow. The first is its journey: Earth goes once round the Sun in a year. The second is its build. It spins about an axis, the line through the North and South Poles. That axis is not upright. It leans 23.4° away from the line that stands at right angles to Earth’s path round the Sun. The lean is called the axial tilt.

Last lesson you saw that the axis keeps pointing at the same spot among the stars, which is why the north celestial pole never moves. That stays true all year round. To see what it means, walk in a circle round a lamp in the middle of a room, holding a pencil at a fixed slant so that it always points the same way. Its top leans towards the lamp when you are on one side of the circle and away from it on the opposite side. On the two sides in between it leans sideways. Earth’s axis does the same round the Sun. Use the buttons to move Earth between three dates.

afterFigure.text: The north end of the axis leans furthest towards the Sun around 21 June and furthest away around 21 December. Those two dates are the solstices. Around 21 March and 22 September it leans sideways, neither towards nor away from the Sun. Those dates are the equinoxes. The next screen shows what the lean does to the Sun’s place in the sky.

lead.text: In the last lesson every star got an address: its declination, the angle north or south of the celestial equator, which is Earth’s equator reaching out to the sky. A star keeps the same declination night after night. The Sun has a declination too, and unlike a star’s it changes through the year. The tilt explains how.

In June the north end of the axis leans towards the Sun, so the Sun lies north of the celestial equator. Its declination is +23.4°, the same number as the tilt. In December the north end leans away and the Sun lies south of the celestial equator, at −23.4°. At the equinoxes the axis leans sideways and the Sun sits on the celestial equator, at 0°. Between those dates the declination slides steadily from one value to the next.

afterFigure.text: Declination also tells you where on Earth a body stands overhead. A star at declination +20° passes straight overhead for anyone at latitude 20° N, because the latitude of a place and the declination of the star above it are the same number. The Sun works the same way. At noon on the June solstice it stands overhead at latitude 23.4° N, a line of latitude called the Tropic of Cancer. At noon on the December solstice it stands overhead at 23.4° S, the Tropic of Capricorn, and at an equinox it stands overhead on the equator. Through the year the place with the noon Sun overhead drifts back and forth between the two tropics, and the size of that journey is measured in degrees of latitude.

lead.text: The two tropics mark the ends of the Sun’s overhead journey, one north of the equator and one south of it.

steps.headline: How high the noon Sun stands

lead.text: Now back to the garden. At noon the place on Earth directly beneath the Sun lies due north or due south of you, on the same line of longitude, so the two of you differ only in latitude. Call your latitude φ and the Sun’s declination δ, as in the last lesson. The gap between you and the place beneath the Sun is then |φ − δ| degrees of latitude. The bars mean the size of the difference, ignoring any minus sign, because a gap is a distance.

Each degree of that gap tips the Sun one degree away from straight overhead. The Sun is so far away that its rays reach every part of Earth along parallel lines, just as the celestial pole lay in the same direction from everywhere. Standing right beneath the Sun, with a gap of 0°, you see it at altitude 90°. Walk one degree of latitude away and it sinks to 89°. That gives the rule for the noon Sun:
Noon altitude of the Sun = 90° − |φ − δ|

afterFigure.text: Try it at 35° N on the June solstice. The Sun’s declination is +23.4°, so the gap is 35° − 23.4° = 11.6° and the noon altitude is 90° − 11.6° = 78.4°. The buttons compare three places on the same date. The further a place lies from the point beneath the Sun, the lower the noon Sun stands.

lead.text: This is the noon Sun over the garden from the opening scene, on the day its shadow was shortest.

reveal.text: A gap of 28.1° of latitude between London and the point beneath the Sun leaves the noon Sun 61.9° up, and a shadow a little over half the stick’s height.

steps.headline: December, and places south of the equator

lead.text: In December the north end of the axis leans away from the Sun, and the Sun’s declination changes sign. It becomes −23.4°, and the rule still works if you keep the signs: latitudes and declinations south of the equator count as negative. Take 40° N on the December solstice. The gap is 40° − (−23.4°) = 63.4°, because subtracting a negative number adds, so the noon altitude is 90° − 63.4° = 26.6°.

The same signs handle places south of the equator, where the seasons are reversed. At 20° S, which is φ = −20°, the June gap is |−20° − 23.4°| = 43.4° and the noon Sun stands 46.6° high. In December the gap is |−20° − (−23.4°)| = 3.4°, and the noon Sun stands 86.6° high, almost overhead.

afterFigure.text: So the Sun is highest over whichever hemisphere is leaning towards it, and London’s lowest noon Sun of the year coincides with the highest for places south of the equator. With the signs in place, the rule gives the noon Sun for any place on either solstice.

lead.text: Back in the garden on the shortest day of December, when the stick’s shadow was at its longest.

reveal.text: A gap of 74.9° leaves the noon Sun only 15.1° up over the garden, and the stick’s shadow stretches to about 3.7 times its height.

steps.headline: How a low Sun spreads its light

lead.text: The two noon heights over the garden, 61.9° in June and 15.1° in December, explain the shadows. They also explain the weather. Sunlight arrives as a broad beam. When the Sun is high, the beam lands almost head-on and covers a small patch of ground. When the Sun is low, the same beam arrives at a slant and is spread over a longer patch, much as a torch held at an angle to a wall lights a stretched oval.

The spreading has a simple size. A beam arriving at altitude h covers 1/sin h times the ground it would cover from overhead, where sin h is the sine of the angle, found on any calculator. At noon in London in June that factor is about 1.1. In December it is about 3.8, so compared with June the same beam is spread over more than three times the ground, and each square metre receives less than a third of the energy.

afterFigure.text: The days differ as well. London has about 16.4 hours of daylight at the June solstice and about 7.6 hours at the December solstice. Winter brings weaker sunlight for fewer hours, and summer brings stronger sunlight for more hours. That combination is what we feel as the seasons.

lead.text: Picture the same torch beam shone onto flat ground, once from high above and once from low down.

A common guess is that summer comes when Earth is nearer the Sun. The numbers disagree. Earth’s distance from the Sun changes by only about 3% over the year, and Earth is nearest in early January, in the middle of the northern winter. When it is summer in London it is winter in Sydney, yet the two cities are the same distance from the Sun on that day. Distance cannot give one place summer and the other winter at the same time.

The tilt gives a better account, and the equinoxes show it most simply. Twice a year the axis leans sideways and the Sun’s declination is 0°. Then the rule becomes 90° − φ, because the gap is simply your latitude. From 25° N the noon Sun stands 65° high at an equinox, and on the equator it passes straight overhead. Day and night each last close to 12 hours everywhere on Earth, which is where the name comes from: equinox means equal night.

afterFigure.text: Everything in this lesson came from one cause. The tilt swings the Sun’s declination north and south, the swing moves the point beneath the Sun, and that point sets the noon height, the spread of the light and the length of the day. The tilt is the only ingredient that changes the Sun’s declination, so there is a way to test the idea: take the tilt away and see what is left.

lead.text: The equinoxes are the simplest dates to use, because the Sun’s declination is a round number.

reveal.text: From 40° N the equinox Sun reaches 50°. From the equator it passes straight overhead.

lead.text: Keep Earth’s spin, orbit and distance exactly as they are. Take away only the tilt.

reveal.text: With the tilt gone, the Sun’s declination stays at 0° and London’s noon Sun keeps one height all year, so the stick’s shadow would never change length.

blocks.text: Push a straight stick upright into level ground in a London garden and come back at noon on the longest day of June. The stick’s shadow is short, a little over half the stick’s height. Come back at noon on the shortest day of December and the shadow has stretched to nearly four times the stick’s height, about seven times as long as in June. The stick and the ground are unchanged, and so is the time of day.

Visit on other days and the tip of the noon shadow slides along one line, creeping out from its nearest mark in June to its farthest in December, then back again. A short shadow means a high Sun and a long one means a low Sun, so the Sun’s path across the sky must change with the seasons.

This lesson finds out how and why. It starts with how Earth travels round the Sun, works out the height of the noon Sun for any place and date, and then turns to what a low Sun does to the weather and whether the tilt really is the cause.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll work out how high the noon Sun stands at any place and date, and say why it changes.

recap.keyIdea: Earth’s tilt swings the Sun’s declination between +23.4° and −23.4° through the year, and the noon Sun stands 90° − |φ − δ| high. That changes how high the Sun climbs and how long the day lasts. Earth’s distance from the Sun plays almost no part.

blocks.text: You began with a stick in a London garden. Its noon Sun stands 61.9° high in June and 15.1° in December, which makes the shadow about half the stick’s height in June and about 3.7 times its height in December. With no tilt the Sun would stay at 38.5° all year and the shadow would never change.

recap.nextHook: The Sun’s cycle takes a year. The Moon’s takes about a month, and its shape changes every night. The next lesson shows how the Moon’s phases come from the angle between Moon and Sun, and why eclipses are so much rarer than new and full moons.

lessons.title: Phases and eclipses

steps.headline: A half-lit ball seen from Earth

lead.text: Hold a ball near a lamp in a dark room and half of it is lit, the half facing the lamp. From the lamp’s side you see the lit half, and from the far side you see only the dark half. The Moon is that ball and the Sun is the lamp, so half the Moon is lit all the time. What we call the Moon’s phase is how much of that lit half happens to face us.

The deciding quantity is an angle. Look at the Sun, then at the Moon, and measure how far round the sky you must turn to get from one to the other, in the direction the Moon travels. Call that angle θ (theta), the Sun–Earth–Moon angle. When θ is 0° the Moon lies in the same direction as the Sun, its lit half faces away from us and we see none of it: new moon. When θ is 180° the Moon lies opposite the Sun and we see all of its lit half: full moon.

afterFigure.text: The trip from one new moon to the next takes about 30 days, and θ grows at close to a steady rate through it. It reaches 180° at full moon, halfway through the cycle, and carries on to 360°, where the Moon is back in the direction of the Sun and a new moon begins. In between come the other phases. A thin lit sliver is a crescent, and a Moon more than half lit is gibbous. The positions a quarter and three quarters of the way round the cycle are the quarter moons.

lead.text: Think about how far round the cycle the Moon has travelled when θ reaches 180°.

steps.headline: How much of the disc is lit

lead.text: Between new moon and full moon the Moon shows some fraction of its disc, and θ fixes that fraction exactly:
Lit fraction of the disc = (1 − cos θ) ÷ 2

Here cos θ is the cosine of the angle, a calculator button that turns an angle into a number between −1 and 1. The rule is easy to test at the two extremes. At θ = 0° the cosine is 1, so the lit fraction is (1 − 1) ÷ 2 = 0 and the disc is dark. At θ = 180° the cosine is −1, so the lit fraction is (1 + 1) ÷ 2 = 1 and the whole disc is lit. In between, the cosine falls smoothly from 1 to −1 and the lit fraction rises smoothly from 0 to 1.

afterFigure.text: Take θ = 150°, a couple of days before full moon. The cosine of 150° is −0.866, so the lit fraction is (1 − (−0.866)) ÷ 2 = 0.933, and 93.3% of the disc is lit. Subtracting a negative number adds, which is why angles past 90° light more than half the disc. Between 180° and 360° the cosine climbs back from −1 to 1, so the Moon runs back through the same fractions in reverse order. While θ grows towards 180° the lit part grows, which is called waxing, and afterwards it shrinks, which is called waning. Any angle now gives a lit fraction.

lead.text: Take the Moon a quarter of the way round its cycle, where the Sun lights it from the side.

reveal.text: The cosine of 90° is 0, so the lit fraction is (1 − 0) ÷ 2, which is half the disc. The Moon is a quarter of the way round its cycle, and that is why it is called a quarter moon.

lead.text: Watch the Moon for several months and the phases keep a steady rhythm. The time from one new moon to the next is 29.53 days, called the synodic month. In that time θ runs once through 360°, which means the Moon gains one full turn on the Sun.

The word gains needs a little care. Both bodies drift eastward across the background of stars. The Sun appears to move about 1° a day because Earth is travelling round its orbit, and the Moon moves about 13° a day. The Moon returns to the same place among the stars after 27.3 days, but by then the Sun has moved on by about 27°, and the Moon needs a little over two more days to catch up. That is why the cycle of phases is longer than the Moon’s own trip round Earth.

afterFigure.text: The gain is steady enough to do arithmetic with. If a full 360° takes 29.53 days, equal angles take equal times: a quarter of the cycle takes a quarter of the time, and halfway round takes half. That lets you turn any angle into a number of days, or any number of days into an angle. Use the slider to run the Moon through its month.

lead.text: Treat the gain as steady across the whole cycle.

reveal.text: That 12.2° of extra turning takes the sky about 49 minutes at 15° an hour, which is why the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each night.

steps.headline: Two ways the Moon meets a shadow

lead.text: Back to the puzzle from the start. Sunlight streaming past Earth leaves a long cone of shadow pointing straight away from the Sun. At full moon the Moon lies on that side of Earth, so it can slip into the cone and darken. That is a lunar eclipse. At new moon the Moon lies on the Sun’s side of Earth, and its own small shadow can fall on Earth’s surface. Anyone standing in that shadow sees the Sun covered, which is a solar eclipse.

Picture a flat sheet of glass with the Sun at the centre and Earth sliding round on it. That sheet is the plane of Earth’s orbit, and the Sun seems to trace its edge across our sky, along a path called the ecliptic. If the Moon also travelled in that sheet, every new moon would sit exactly between Earth and the Sun and every full moon would sit exactly in Earth’s shadow.

afterFigure.text: We would then see a solar eclipse at every new moon and a lunar eclipse at every full moon. We do not, so the Moon cannot be travelling in the sheet. The next screen shows how it travels instead.

lead.text: The Moon’s path round Earth is a hoop with Earth at its centre, tilted by 5.1° to the glass sheet. Half of the hoop lies above the sheet and half below, and the Moon crosses the sheet twice in each orbit.

A tilt of 5.1° sounds small, but at the Moon’s distance it lifts the Moon more than 30,000 km clear of the sheet at the highest and lowest points of its path. The shadows lie along the sheet, so most months the Moon passes above or below Earth’s shadow at full moon, and above or below the Sun at new moon. An eclipse needs a new or full moon to happen while the Moon is close to the sheet: within about 1° of the ecliptic for a lunar eclipse and about 1.5° for a solar one, in the model drawn here. Use the buttons to compare a full moon that sits on the ecliptic with two that miss.

afterFigure.text: Eclipses come only in the short spells, about twice a year, when the Moon crosses the sheet near a new or full moon.

cases.label: Full moon 4.5° north of the ecliptic
New moon 3° south of the ecliptic

lead.text: Think about which side of Earth the shadow cone points to.

reveal.text: Earth’s shadow points away from the Sun, so the Moon must be on the far side of Earth. Even then it must lie within about 1° of the ecliptic in this model, so most full moons miss.

steps.headline: The Moon’s size against the Sun’s

lead.text: One more thing decides whether a solar eclipse can black out the Sun completely: the Moon has to look at least as big as the Sun. How big something looks is its angular size, also called its angular diameter, the angle between the lines of sight to its two edges. It depends on how wide the object is and on how far away it is.

For a small angle there is a simple rule. The angular size in radians is the diameter divided by the distance. A radian is a unit for angles, equal to about 57.3°, so multiplying by 57.3 gives degrees. The rule shows how a small body close by and a big body far away can look the same size.

afterFigure.text: Seen from Earth the Sun spans about 0.53°. It is roughly 400 times wider than the Moon but also roughly 400 times further away, so the two sizes should come out close. That leaves the Moon’s own numbers to put into the rule.

lead.text: Use the Moon’s average distance, and treat the angle as small.

reveal.text: The Moon spans 0.52°, almost exactly the Sun’s 0.53°. That match is why a new moon on the ecliptic can just cover the Sun’s bright disc. The Moon’s distance varies by a few percent, so it sometimes covers the Sun completely and sometimes leaves a thin ring of light round the edge.

blocks.text: On a clear evening a thin silver curve sometimes hangs low in the west just after sunset. A week later the Moon stands high in the south at dusk, half of its face lit. After another week the full Moon rises just as the Sun sets and stays up all night. A week after that a half-lit Moon rises around midnight. By the end of the month it has shrunk to a sliver in the dawn sky and then vanished.

The Moon makes no light of its own. The Sun lights it, and the Sun always lights the half that faces it, whatever shape we see. So the changing shape has to come from where the Moon is on its path round Earth. This lesson works out how, and how long the cycle takes.

The month also raises a puzzle. At new moon the Moon lies in the direction of the Sun, and at full moon it lies directly opposite, yet the Sun is not blotted out every month and the full moon is not darkened every month. The last screens find out why.

lessons.title: Kepler's laws

steps.headline: A circle that has been stretched

lead.text: Take a loop of string, push two pins into a sheet of paper and slip the loop over both. Hold the string tight with a pencil and slide the pencil round, keeping the string taut. The curve you draw is an ellipse, a circle stretched out along one direction. Each pin marks a focus (the plural is foci), and the two pins are what shape the curve. Put them close together and the ellipse is almost a circle. Pull them apart and it grows long and thin.

afterFigure.text: Kepler’s first discovery was that Mars follows an ellipse, and so does every other planet. The Sun is not at the middle of the ellipse. It sits at one of the foci, and the other focus is empty. That small shift matters, because it means a planet is nearer the Sun at one end of its path than at the other. The next screens put numbers on the shape.

lead.text: Start with the size. The longest line you can draw across an ellipse runs through both foci, and it is called the long axis. Half of it is the semi-major axis, written a, and it is the number astronomers use for the size of an orbit. For a circle it is simply the radius.

Because the Sun lies on that line, a planet passes it twice in every orbit. The point nearest the Sun is perihelion and the point farthest from it is aphelion. We measure distances in the solar system in astronomical units: 1 AU is the average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km.

afterFigure.text: The two ends of the long axis are perihelion and aphelion, with the Sun somewhere between them. So the long axis is the perihelion distance plus the aphelion distance, and the semi-major axis is half of that sum. A comet that comes within 3 AU of the Sun and swings out to 9 AU has a long axis of 12 AU, so its semi-major axis is 6 AU.

lead.text: The Sun lies on the long axis, between its two ends.

The semi-major axis says how big an orbit is but not how stretched it is, and two ellipses with the same a can look very different. The stretch is the eccentricity, written e. A circle has e = 0 because it is not stretched at all, and the nearer e gets to 1 the longer and thinner the ellipse becomes. Every planet’s orbit falls between 0 and 1.

The eccentricity also says how far the Sun sits from the middle of the orbit. The gap between the centre and the Sun is a × e. For a circle that gap is zero, so the Sun is at the centre. For a long, thin ellipse the Sun sits close to one end.

afterFigure.text: That gap gives us both ends of the orbit. Measured from the Sun, the near end is a − a × e, which is a(1 − e), and the far end is a + a × e, which is a(1 + e). Earth’s e is only 0.017, so its distance from the Sun changes by about 3% over the year. An asteroid with a large e swings much farther.

steps.headline: Find the aphelion distance when a = 3 AU and e = 0.5.

workedSteps.text: The far end is the centre-to-Sun gap, a × e, beyond a.
Put in the numbers.
Calculate.

lead.text: Now the near end. The gap from the centre to the Sun has to come off a.

reveal.text: You took the Sun’s gap off a, so the near end is a(1 − e). The stretch e pulls the closest point in from a by the fraction e.

lead.text: Distances give the shape. The speed is the next question, and Kepler found that a planet does not move at a steady rate. It speeds up as it nears the Sun and slows as it moves away.

Picture a line from the Sun to the planet. As the planet moves, the line sweeps across the orbit like the hand of a clock sweeping across the dial. Kepler’s second law says that this line sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Over one month it covers the same area whether the planet is near the Sun or far from it.

afterFigure.text: That rule forces the change of speed. A short line sweeps out a given area only if the planet covers a long stretch of its path, while a long line sweeps out the same area over a short stretch. So near the Sun the planet moves quickly and far from it the planet moves slowly. At the two ends of the long axis the speeds are in the inverse ratio of the distances: half the distance means twice the speed.

lead.text: Use the near and far distances you found for this asteroid.

reveal.text: The asteroid is four times faster at perihelion than at aphelion. Equal areas in equal times makes the speed change by this much.

lead.text: The last rule links the size of an orbit to the time it takes. The period, P, is the time a planet needs to go once round. A planet on a bigger orbit has further to go, so it takes longer. The question is how much longer.

Kepler’s third law gives the answer: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Measure P in years and a in AU for a planet orbiting the Sun, and the law becomes P² = a³. Earth has a = 1 AU and P = 1 year, which fits. Mars has a = 1.52 AU, so P² = 1.52³ = 3.51 and P is about 1.87 years.

afterFigure.text: A planet’s period depends only on a. Two orbits with the same semi-major axis take the same time, whatever their stretch. Time grows quickly with size: an orbit four times as wide takes eight times as long, because a planet on a wider orbit has more path to cover and also moves more slowly along it.

lead.text: Cube the semi-major axis to get P², then take the square root.

So far the Sun has been in charge, and P² = a³ is the law for anything that orbits the Sun, in years and AU. Around another star the numbers change. A heavier star pulls harder, so a planet at the same distance has to move faster to avoid falling in, and it finishes its orbit sooner.
Astronomers count a star’s mass in solar masses, with the Sun as 1. For a star of M solar masses the third law becomes P² = a³ ÷ M. Put M = 1 and you get the Sun’s law back.

afterFigure.text: With a star of 9 solar masses and a planet at 1 AU, P² = 1³ ÷ 9 = 1/9, so P is 1/3 of a year. That is four months. Around the Sun the same orbit takes a full year, so the heavier star has shortened the period without changing the size of the orbit.

lead.text: Use the star’s mass in solar masses in P² = a³ ÷ M.

reveal.text: The star’s extra mass divides P² by 4, so the period halves. A stronger pull needs a faster orbit, and the planet gets round sooner.

lessons.orientation: Describe an orbit by its size and shape, and link its period to its semi-major axis.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In 1600 Johannes Kepler joined Tycho Brahe, who had spent decades writing down where the planets stand in the sky, night after night, without a telescope. Kepler took the records for Mars and tried to find the path it follows round the Sun. Everyone expected a circle, because a circle seemed the only shape fit for the heavens.

Circle after circle failed. Each one came close, then missed Mars by about a quarter of the width of the Full Moon. Tycho’s measurements were better than that, so Kepler trusted the records and gave up the circle. What he found in its place still describes every orbit, from Earth’s to a comet’s.

He found three rules. The first gives the shape of an orbit and the second the speed along it. The third links the size of an orbit to the time it takes to go round. We will take them one at a time, starting with the shape.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll find an orbit’s closest and farthest points and use its size to work out how long it takes to go round.

recap.keyIdea: A planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, fastest at perihelion. Its period in years and semi-major axis in AU satisfy P² = a³.

blocks.text: You began with Kepler failing to fit a circle to Mars. You found that an orbit running from 1 AU to 9 AU has a long axis of 10 AU, and that an asteroid with a = 2 AU and e = 0.6 moves four times faster at perihelion than at aphelion. A 4 AU orbit takes 8 years, and a planet at 1 AU around a star of four solar masses needs only half a year.

recap.nextHook: Kepler described how the planets move without saying why they move that way. The next lesson follows Newton as he asks what pulls a planet along its orbit, starting with a falling apple and the Moon.

lessons.title: Newton's gravitation

steps.headline: From the apple to the Moon

lead.text: Newton’s idea was that gravity weakens with distance, and the odd number from the opening tells us by how much. The Moon is about 60 times as far from Earth’s centre as the apple is. Square 60 and you get 3,600. If the pull falls as the square of the distance, then at 60 times the distance it is 60 × 60 = 3,600 times weaker, which is exactly the drop in the Moon’s fall.
This is called an inverse-square law. Double the distance and the pull falls to a quarter, because 2 × 2 = 4. Triple it and the pull falls to a ninth.

afterFigure.text: Newton did not take this from theory alone. It is the one rule that fits the falling apple, the Moon and the planets together. The arrows in the drawing share a single scale, so you can watch the force shrink as the two bodies move apart.

lead.text: Apply the same rule to two bodies that are pulled three times as far apart.

reveal.text: You tripled the separation, so the pull fell by 3 × 3 = 9. Gravity follows the square of the distance.

lead.text: Distance is only part of the story, because gravity also depends on how much matter is doing the pulling. Double the mass of the body that pulls and the force doubles. Double the mass of the body being pulled and the force doubles again, which is why a heavier person weighs more. The force depends on the product of the two masses.

Call the masses M and m, and the distance between their centres r. Newton’s law is F = GMm/r². G is the gravitational constant, 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², a fixed number that sets the scale. It is so small that you feel the pull of a whole planet but not of the person beside you.

afterFigure.text: One more fact comes with the law. The pull is shared: when Earth pulls on the Moon with a force F, the Moon pulls back on Earth with exactly the same force, in the opposite direction. The Moon is far more affected because a given force changes the motion of a light body much more than that of a heavy one.

steps.headline: By what factor does the force change when r is halved and one mass is doubled?

workedSteps.text: Halving r multiplies the force by the square of 2.
Doubling one mass multiplies the force by 2.
Each change acts on its own, so the factors multiply.

lead.text: Here the separation stays fixed. Only the masses change.

reveal.text: Each mass scales the pull on its own, so you multiplied the two factors.

steps.headline: What the pull does to a falling object

lead.text: Now apply the law to something falling. The pull on a mass m near a body of mass M is GMm/r². How fast the object speeds up depends on that pull divided by its own mass, because a heavier object needs a bigger push to change its motion by the same amount. Divide by m and the m cancels: g = GM/r².

The result g is an acceleration, the amount by which the object’s speed grows each second. It is called the gravitational field of the body at that place, and 9.8 m/s² would mean a falling object is 9.8 m/s faster after every second.

afterFigure.text: M is the mass of the body doing the pulling (Earth, for example) and r is the distance from its centre. Because the falling object’s own mass has dropped out, every object at that place gets the same acceleration, whatever its weight.

lead.text: At the surface of a world, r is the world’s radius, so g = GM/R². Each world has its own GM, the product of G and its mass. The units matter: GM is in m³/s², so the radius has to be in metres.

Take the Moon, with GM = 4.90 × 10¹² m³/s² and a radius of 1,737 km, which is 1.737 × 10⁶ m. The radius squared is 3.017 × 10¹² m², and dividing GM by it gives g = 1.62 m/s². That is far weaker than the pull you feel on Earth.

afterFigure.text: Two things set the surface gravity of a world. More mass raises it, and a larger radius lowers it, by the square, because the surface is then farther from the centre. A small world can have weak gravity even when it is dense, and a large world can have strong gravity even when it is light.

lead.text: Use SI units. GM is in m³/s², so convert the radius from kilometres to metres before you square it.

reveal.text: That is how fast any object gains speed near Earth’s surface. The same formula gave the Moon’s value from its own GM and radius.

lead.text: The field g = GM/r² applies to any planet. Take a planet with Earth’s mass but twice Earth’s radius.

reveal.text: Doubling r with the mass fixed divides g by four. The same inverse-square rule governs the Moon’s fall and a planet’s surface.

lessons.orientation: Use the inverse-square law of gravity to compare forces and compute surface gravity.

blocks.text: Isaac Newton is said to have been sitting in a garden when an apple dropped from a tree. Whether or not it happened that way, the thought he took from it was that Earth’s pull might not stop at the treetops. It might reach all the way to the Moon, and be the very thing that keeps the Moon from flying off in a straight line.

The numbers pointed that way. An apple drops about 5 m in its first second. The Moon is falling too, in its own fashion: without Earth’s pull it would sail off in a straight line, and each second it drops about 1.4 mm below that line. The Moon is about 60 times as far from Earth’s centre as the apple is, yet its fall is not 60 times smaller. It is about 3,600 times smaller.

That odd number turned out to be the key. This lesson follows Newton from it to a law that covers every pair of masses in the universe, and then uses the law to find how strongly gravity pulls on Earth and on other worlds.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll use F = GMm/r² to say how gravity changes with distance and mass, and to find g.

recap.keyIdea: Gravity pulls every pair of masses with F = GMm/r². The force falls as the square of the separation, and g = GM/r² is the same for every falling object.

blocks.text: You began with the gap between the apple’s fall and the Moon’s, and saw that 60² = 3,600 accounts for it. You found that tripling the separation cuts the pull to a ninth, and that at Earth’s surface g is 9.82 m/s².

recap.nextHook: One law covers the falling apple and the Moon. The next lesson asks how fast something must be thrown to stay in orbit, and how fast to leave Earth altogether.

lessons.title: Orbits, escape and tides

lead.text: Two numbers decide what happens to the cannonball. The first is how far it falls: anything dropped near the ground falls about 5 m in its first second, whatever its sideways speed. The second is the shape of the ground. Earth is round, so its surface curves away from a straight line by about 5 m for every 8 km you travel along it.

Put the two together. A ball that travels 8 km while it falls 5 m finds the ground has dropped away by 5 m beneath it, so it is no closer to the surface than when it started. A second later the same thing happens again.

afterFigure.text: Fire the ball more slowly and the ground catches it. Fire it faster and its path stretches into a long ellipse, as Kepler found for the planets. At one particular speed the path is a circle, and the ball keeps falling round the Earth without ever landing. Using the two numbers above, you can work out what that speed is.

lead.text: Compare how far the ball drops in one second with how far the ground drops away.

reveal.text: You matched the 5 m the ball falls to the 5 m the ground curves away. Covering 8 km each second does that, and that is an orbit.

lead.text: That 8 km/s is for a ball skimming Earth, and the same reasoning works at any height. A body moving at speed v on a circle of radius r has to be pulled inward by v²/r each second to stay on the circle. Gravity supplies GM/r². Set the two equal and you get v² = GM/r, so the circular speed is v = √(GM/r).
Here r is measured from the centre of the body, not from the ground. It has to be in metres because GM is in m³/s².

afterFigure.text: Two things follow. The farther out you are, the larger r is and the slower the circular speed, so high satellites move more slowly than low ones. And a body that is slower than the circular speed at its height is pulled in faster than its path curves away, so it falls to the ground. A faster body swings out into an ellipse.

steps.headline: Find the circular speed at the Moon's distance, 384,400 km from Earth's centre.

workedSteps.text: Write r in metres.
Divide GM by r.
Take the square root.

lead.text: Measure r from Earth’s centre, not from the ground. Work in metres, as in the example.

reveal.text: Almost 8 km/s, the same speed as in the ball puzzle, now from the formula. At that speed the ground curves away as fast as you fall.

lead.text: The same formula works for planets around the Sun. Use the Sun’s GM and Earth’s distance from the Sun.

reveal.text: 29.8 km/s matches NASA’s measured mean of 29.78 km/s. One formula serves satellites and planets.

lead.text: Fire the ball faster than the circular speed and its ellipse stretches longer and longer. At one speed the far end never arrives: the path opens out and the ball never returns. That is the escape speed, v = √(2GM/r).
The escape speed is always √2 times the circular speed at the same distance, about 1.41 times, wherever you are.

afterFigure.text: The ball can get away with a finite speed because the pull weakens as it climbs, and by the time it is far enough out there is hardly any left. The escape speed does not depend on the direction of the launch or on the ball’s own mass. It depends only on the body you are leaving and on how far you start from its centre. The square root of 2 under the root sign is the only change from the circular speed formula.

lead.text: From the surface, r is Earth’s radius. The formula is the same as before, with a 2 under the root.

reveal.text: About 11 km/s, √2 times the speed that merely skims the surface. Air resistance is ignored.

steps.headline: A pull that differs across Earth

lead.text: Gravity can also stretch a body. The Moon pulls on all of Earth, but not equally. The ocean on the Moon’s side is nearer to the Moon than Earth’s centre is, and Earth’s centre is nearer than the ocean on the far side. So the pull is strongest on the near water and weakest on the far water.

Compared with the centre of Earth, the near water is pulled towards the Moon and the far water is left behind. The oceans are stretched into two bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. As Earth turns through them, a coast sees two high tides a day.

afterFigure.text: The size of the stretch depends on how much the pull changes from one side of Earth to the other. A difference in pull falls faster than the pull itself, as the cube of the distance. Put the Moon three times as far away and the stretch would drop to a 27th. Closer in, it would grow just as quickly.

cases.label: The Moon at its present distance
The Moon at about twice the distance

lead.text: The Sun raises tides too. It pulls far harder than the Moon, but it is so much farther away that its stretch is only 0.46 of the Moon’s.

The two stretches add or partly cancel, depending on where the Sun lies. At new moon and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line and the bulges build on each other. These are the biggest tides of the month, called spring tides, though they have nothing to do with the season. At the quarter moons the Sun is at right angles to the Moon and the stretches partly cancel, so the tides are smallest. These are neap tides.

afterFigure.text: Look at the two drawings. In the first the Sun and Moon pull along the same line, and in the second they pull across each other.

lead.text: Tides come from a difference in pull, and the Moon’s pull on Earth changes with distance.

reveal.text: A difference in pull falls as the cube of the distance, so halving the distance multiplies the tide by 8. The Sun’s tide is 0.46 of the Moon’s.

cases.label: Moon today, Sun at right angles

lessons.orientation: Compute circular and escape speeds and explain tides as a difference in pull.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Newton pictured a cannon on top of a very high mountain. Fire a ball gently and it drops to the ground a short way off. Fire it harder and it lands farther away. Whatever its sideways speed, the ball falls about 5 m in its first second.

Now fire it so hard that it travels a very long way before it lands. Earth is round, so the ground curves away below the ball. Far enough along, the ground has dropped away by as much as the ball has fallen, and the ball is no nearer the surface than before. Fired fast enough, it keeps falling and keeps missing the ground, all the way round the world.

That ball is in orbit, and it is what the Moon is doing. This lesson finds the speed that keeps a ball in orbit and the larger speed that frees it from Earth altogether. It then turns to something gravity does to the oceans.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll find the speeds for orbiting and escaping, and say why tides depend on distance cubed.

recap.keyIdea: Gravity sets the speed that keeps a circular orbit, √(GM/r), and the escape speed, √2 times larger. Tides come from a difference in pull, which falls as 1/d³.

blocks.text: You began with a ball that keeps missing the ground and found that it needs about 8 km/s. A satellite 400 km up needs 7.67 km/s, and escaping Earth takes 11.19 km/s. Tides depend on the cube of the distance, so halving the Moon’s distance would multiply them by 8.

recap.nextHook: Orbits and tides tell us how much mass is pulling. The next lesson turns from motion to light and asks how the brightness of a star can tell us how far away it is.

lessons.title: Brightness and distance

lead.text: Go back to the torch. Its beam is a cone, so the lit circle widens in step with the distance. At 2 m the circle is twice as wide as at 1 m. The area of a circle depends on its width multiplied by itself, so a circle twice as wide covers 2 × 2 = 4 times the area.
The torch gives out the same amount of light at either distance. At 2 m that light is spread over four times the area, so every patch of wall receives a quarter of what it did at 1 m.

afterFigure.text: Brightness on the wall falls with the square of the distance. Gravity follows the same square rule. The two drawings show the Sun’s light at 1 AU and at 2 AU.

lead.text: Use the same rule: the width grows with the distance, and the area with the width multiplied by itself.
A star works like the torch, except that its light goes out in every direction. Instead of a circle on a wall, the light at distance d has spread over a whole sphere of area 4πd².

Astronomers keep two quantities apart. A star’s luminosity, L, is the total power it gives out, measured in watts. The Sun’s is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W. The flux, F, is the power that arrives on each square metre facing the star, so F = L ÷ 4πd².

afterFigure.text: Luminosity belongs to the star and does not change with distance. Flux is what a telescope measures, and it does change: double the distance and the same light covers four times the area, so the flux falls to a quarter. Everything in this lesson comes from comparing those two quantities.

steps.headline: How much solar flux reaches Jupiter, 5 AU from the Sun?

workedSteps.text: Write the distance in metres.
Find the area of the sphere the light has spread over.
Divide the luminosity by that area.

lead.text: Use SI units, so the distance is in metres. The Sun’s luminosity is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W.

reveal.text: About 1,361 W on every square metre facing the Sun, above the atmosphere. That figure is called the solar constant.

steps.headline: A yearly shift in the sky

lead.text: Flux gives a distance only if we already know the luminosity, and for most stars we do not. We need a way to measure distance directly. Hold a finger at arm’s length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps against the background, and the nearer the finger, the bigger the jump.

Earth does the same thing as it moves. Six months apart it stands on opposite sides of its orbit, 2 AU apart, and a nearby star seems to shift against the far more distant stars behind it. Half of the full shift is the star’s parallax, p. The shifts are tiny, so they are measured in arcseconds, and an arcsecond is a 3,600th of a degree.

afterFigure.text: Astronomers define a parsec as the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond. It is 206,265 AU, or 3.26 light-years. A larger shift means a nearer star, and the rule is d = 1/p, with d in parsecs and p in arcseconds. A star with p = 0.5 arcseconds is 2 parsecs away.

lead.text: A larger shift means a nearer star. Use d = 1/p.

reveal.text: You turned a shift of less than one arcsecond into a distance of 1.30 pc, about 4.25 light-years.

lead.text: Now the two methods help each other. Parallax gives the distance d, and a telescope gives the flux F. Rearrange F = L ÷ 4πd² and you get L = 4πd²F. A star’s true power follows from two measurements.

This also shows why brightness alone misleads. Equal flux needs L ÷ d² to match, so a feeble star close by and a powerful star far away can look the same. A star 16 times as luminous as another looks equally bright when it is 4 times farther away, because 4 × 4 = 16.

afterFigure.text: The distance grows only as the square root of the luminosity. That is why astronomers want a parallax before they say how powerful a star is.

lead.text: Flux is proportional to L ÷ d², so a change in luminosity and a change in distance both alter it.

reveal.text: Equal flux needs L ÷ d² to match, so d grows as the square root of L. Once parallax gives d, the measured flux gives L = 4πd²F.

lessons.orientation: Apply the inverse-square law to starlight and measure distance by parallax.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Hold a torch 1 m from a wall and it lights a circle. Step back to 3 m and the circle grows, though the torch has not changed at all. The same light now covers a wider patch of wall, so each part of the wall gets less of it and the patch looks dimmer.

Stars are like torches that nobody can walk up to. A star that looks faint may be a feeble light close by or a blazing one very far away, and looking at it does not say which. Astronomers first need a way to measure the distance. Then they need a way to turn the brightness they see into the star’s true power.
This lesson gets both. We start with the torch and the wall, follow the light out to the stars, and then use the way a nearby star seems to shift through the year to measure how far away it is.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll find a star’s distance from its parallax and its luminosity from its brightness.

recap.keyIdea: A star's flux is its luminosity spread over a sphere, F = L/(4πd²). Parallax gives the distance, and with the distance the flux gives the luminosity.

blocks.text: You began with a torch on a wall and found that at 3 m its light covers 9 times the area. The Sun delivers 1,361 W/m² at Earth, and Proxima Centauri, with a parallax of 0.768 arcseconds, is 1.30 pc away.

recap.nextHook: Distance and brightness give a star’s true power. The next lesson reads two more messages in starlight: its colour, which gives its temperature, and the shift of its spectral lines, which gives its speed.

lessons.title: Temperature, colour and motion

lead.text: Anything hot enough glows, and the light it gives off is a mix of wavelengths. The wavelength of light decides its colour: red light has a long wavelength and blue light a short one. We measure wavelengths in nanometres (nm), a billionth of a metre, and visible light runs from about 400 nm for violet to about 700 nm for red.

A glowing object does not give out all wavelengths equally. Its light has a peak, one wavelength at which it shines most strongly, and the rest tails away on either side. An object that glows only because it is hot is called a blackbody. Stars behave almost like blackbodies.

afterFigure.text: The peak moves with temperature, as it did in the poker. A hotter object has a peak at a shorter wavelength, so it looks bluer. A cooler one peaks at a longer wavelength and looks redder. The Sun’s peak is in the blue-green, but it also gives out plenty at every other visible wavelength, and the mix looks white.

lead.text: There is an exact rule for how the peak moves, and it is called Wien’s law: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T. Here λmax (lambda-max) is the peak wavelength in metres and T is the temperature in kelvin. The kelvin scale counts from absolute zero, so a temperature in kelvin is the Celsius temperature plus 273.

The law divides by T, so a hotter object has a smaller λmax. Double the temperature and the peak wavelength halves. You can try it on yourself: your skin is at about 310 K, which puts your peak at about 9,350 nm, well beyond red light. That is why thermal cameras, which sense those long wavelengths, can see people in the dark.

afterFigure.text: Run the law in either direction. From a temperature you can find the colour, and from a measured peak you can work out how hot a star’s surface is, without going anywhere near it. The next example takes one star from temperature to wavelength.

steps.headline: Find the peak wavelength of a star with a surface temperature of 9,000 K.

workedSteps.text: Divide Wien's constant by the temperature.
Convert metres to nanometres by multiplying by 10⁹.
Compare with visible light, which runs from about 400 to 700 nm.

lead.text: Same law, with the Sun’s surface temperature. Give the peak in nanometres.

reveal.text: The Sun’s peak is in the blue-green, but it emits right across the visible range, so it looks white.

lead.text: Run Wien’s law backwards: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ λmax. Write λmax in metres.

reveal.text: A peak at 290 nm lies in the ultraviolet. Hot stars such as Vega, near 10,000 K, look blue-white.

lead.text: Starlight carries a second message. Pass it through a prism and spread it into a rainbow, called a spectrum, and thin dark or bright spectral lines appear at particular wavelengths. Each kind of atom makes lines at its own wavelengths, which can be measured in a laboratory. Hydrogen has one at 656.28 nm, in the red. The lines are like fingerprints that name the atoms in a star.

Now suppose the star is moving away from us. Each wave is sent out from a point a little farther off than the wave before, so the waves reach us stretched. Every line moves to a longer wavelength. If the star is coming towards us the waves are squeezed, and the lines move to shorter wavelengths.

afterFigure.text: A shift to longer wavelengths is a redshift, and a shift to shorter ones is a blueshift. It is the same effect as a siren dropping in pitch once the ambulance has passed. The faster the star moves, the bigger the stretch, and what counts is the stretch as a fraction of the original wavelength.

lead.text: Compare how much the wavelength grew with the wavelength it started with.

The fraction by which a line is stretched equals the star’s speed as a fraction of the speed of light: Δλ ÷ λ = v ÷ c. Rearranged, v = cΔλ/λ. Here Δλ (delta lambda) is the observed wavelength minus the laboratory wavelength, λ is the laboratory wavelength, and c is the speed of light, 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s. A positive Δλ means the star is receding and a negative one means it is approaching.
The rule holds for speeds well below the speed of light, which covers every star in our galaxy.

afterFigure.text: A line stretched by 0.5% means a speed of 0.5% of c, which is 1,500 km/s. Only motion along the line of sight shifts the lines. A star moving sideways across the sky produces no shift at all, so the method gives a star’s radial velocity and nothing else.

lead.text: Δλ is the observed wavelength minus the laboratory one. Positive means receding.

reveal.text: A shift of about 1% of the wavelength means a speed of about 1% of c. That is how astronomers measure the speeds of stars and galaxies they will never visit.

lead.text: Stars in our galaxy move at tens to hundreds of kilometres per second, so their shifts are tiny. An approaching source has a negative radial velocity.

reveal.text: The line moves 0.25 nm towards the blue. Only motion along the line of sight shows up.

lessons.orientation: Read a star's temperature from its colour and its motion from shifted spectral lines.

blocks.text: Watch a metal poker heat in a fire. At first it is dull and dark. Then it glows dull red, then orange, then yellow-white. The hotter the metal gets, the bluer the light becomes, and you can tell roughly how hot it is without touching it.

Stars give out light in the same way. Some look orange-red and others blue-white, even to the naked eye. That difference is one of temperature. Their light also carries a second message: when a star moves, its light changes slightly, as a siren drops in pitch when an ambulance passes you.
This lesson reads both messages. We start with colour and the temperature it gives, then move on to the change that gives a star’s speed along our line of sight.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll read a star’s temperature from its colour and its speed from the shift in its spectral lines.

recap.keyIdea: A star's colour gives its temperature through Wien's law, and the shift of its spectral lines gives its speed along our line of sight, v = cΔλ/λ.

blocks.text: You began with a glowing poker and found that a star’s colour gives its temperature. The Sun peaks at 502 nm, a peak at 290 nm means about 10,000 K, and a line stretched by 1% means a speed of 1% of the speed of light.

recap.nextHook: Temperature and brightness are two measurements of every star. The next lesson plots one against the other and finds that the stars do not fall just anywhere.

lessons.title: The H–R diagram

steps.headline: Size and the glow of a surface

lead.text: Start with an electric hob. Every patch of a glowing ring gives out heat and light, so a wide ring gives out more in total than a narrow one at the same temperature. The extra comes from having more glowing surface.

A star behaves the same way. Its whole surface glows, and two stars at the same surface temperature shine equally on every square metre, so the one with more surface gives out more light. The measure of size to use is the radius, the distance from the centre of the star to its surface.

A sphere has a surface area of 4πR², which grows with the square of the radius. Make a star three times as wide and its surface is 3 × 3 = 9 times as large, so at the same temperature it is 9 times as luminous. The rule also runs backwards. A star that is 9 times as luminous as another at the same temperature must be 3 times as wide, because 3 is the number that multiplies by itself to give 9.
Use the surface-area rule from the last screen. At the same temperature, the light a star gives out follows its surface.

reveal.text: Doubling the radius gives four times the surface, and at the same temperature that is four times the light.

lead.text: Surface area is only half of the story. The other half is how brightly each square metre shines, and that depends strongly on temperature. A white-hot poker gives out far more light than a dull red one, though it is the same poker.

Measurements of glowing surfaces show that each square metre gives out power in proportion to T⁴, the temperature multiplied by itself four times. Make a surface three times hotter and every square metre shines 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81 times as brightly.

Put the two halves together by counting in solar units. Measure the radius in solar radii (R☉), so the Sun has R = 1. Compare the temperature with the Sun's 5,772 K, written T☉. Measure luminosity in solar luminosities (L☉), so the Sun gives 1 L☉. Then L = R² × (T/T☉)⁴.

The radius is squared and the temperature is raised to the fourth power, so temperature is the stronger lever. The formula also works backwards. Divide a luminosity by R², then take the fourth root of what is left to find T/T☉. A star with the Sun's radius that shines at 81 L☉ has T/T☉ = 3, because 3⁴ = 81.
This star has the Sun's radius, so R² = 1 and only the temperature changes the answer.

reveal.text: Doubling the temperature multiplies the luminosity by 2⁴, so temperature is a far stronger lever than radius.

steps.headline: Find the luminosity of a star with R = 2 R☉ and T = 1.5 T☉.

lead.text: Now the chart can be built properly. Each star becomes one dot. Its temperature decides how far across the dot sits and its luminosity decides how high. Luminosity covers an enormous range, from a ten-thousandth of the Sun's to a million times it, so each step up the side is a hundred times the one below. The temperature scale is squeezed in the same way.

There is one oddity. Temperature runs backwards, with the hottest stars on the left and the coolest on the right. Astronomers inherited that order from an older system that sorted stars by their spectra from hottest to coolest, and they kept it. A chart of luminosity against temperature drawn this way is called an H–R diagram, after Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell, who drew the first ones in the early 1910s.

afterFigure.text: Look at where the dots fall. They do not spread over the page. Most stars, the Sun among them, lie along a broad band that slants from hot and luminous at the top left down to cool and dim at the bottom right. About nine stars in ten belong to this band, which is called the main sequence.

Sirius A, hotter than the Sun, sits above and to the left of it. Proxima Centauri, cooler, sits well below and to the right. Along the main sequence the hotter stars are also the larger ones, so both factors in the formula push the luminosity the same way.

lead.text: Some dots lie well away from the band, and the formula says what those stars must be. Take the top right, where the stars are cool and yet very luminous. A cool surface gives out little light per square metre, so a star there can only be that luminous by having an enormous surface. These are giants and supergiants, with radii from tens to hundreds of times the Sun's.

Now take the bottom left, where the stars are hot and yet dim. A hot surface shines fiercely per square metre, so for the star to be dim it must have very little surface. These are white dwarfs, hot stars about the size of Earth and far smaller than the Sun.

afterFigure.text: The faint slanting lines in the picture join stars of the same radius. They slope down towards the right, and the larger the radius, the higher the line lies. So position on the chart gives a star's size as well as its heat.

One consequence is worth keeping. Stars of equal temperature sit in a vertical line, and every square metre of their surfaces shines equally. Going up that line has to mean more surface, so at a fixed temperature, height on the chart measures size.

lead.text: This supergiant is cool but huge. Its radius is squared and its temperature ratio is raised to the fourth power, and the two factors pull against each other.

reveal.text: A cool surface alone would make the star dim. Only an enormous radius gives it tens of thousands of times the Sun's output.

lead.text: A white dwarf is hot but tiny. Its small radius shrinks R² a great deal, while its hot surface raises the temperature factor.

reveal.text: A star the size of Earth, yet hotter than the Sun, gives out only a few hundredths of the Sun's power.

lead.text: Two stars are plotted at the same temperature, one far above the other on the chart.

reveal.text: Equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so extra luminosity has to come from extra surface area. Height on the diagram at fixed temperature measures size.

blocks.text: By now every star has two numbers beside its name. One is its surface temperature, which the colour of its light gives you. The other is its luminosity, the total light it gives out, which you can work out once you know how far away it is. Astronomers have both numbers for many thousands of stars, and a table that long is hard to make sense of.

So try drawing it. Rule a sheet of paper, put temperature along the bottom and luminosity up the side, and mark one dot for every star. If temperature and luminosity were unrelated, the dots would scatter over the whole page like salt on a table. They don't. Most of them fall along one slanting band, and a few strays sit in the empty corners.

The strays are the interesting ones. Before reading the chart we need to know what puts a star at a particular spot, and that comes down to how big the star is and how hot its surface is. We start with those two, then build the chart and read it.

blocks.text: You started with a table of stars and found what sets each star's place on the chart. Doubling the radius gives four times the light, doubling the temperature gives sixteen times, and a cool supergiant of 760 R☉ shines at about 87,000 L☉.

recap.nextHook: Most stars lie on the main sequence, and what places a star on that band is its mass. The next lesson follows a star's mass to the length of its life.

lessons.title: How mass sets a star's life

lead.text: Take a car with a full tank. How far it goes depends on two things, the size of the tank and how fast the engine drinks. A big tank feeding a thirsty engine can run dry sooner than a small tank feeding a frugal one. The time until empty is the fuel divided by the rate of use.

A star has both. On the main sequence it makes its light by fusion in its core, where hydrogen nuclei are squeezed together hot enough to join into helium and release energy. The hydrogen in the core is the tank. The rate of burning is the star's luminosity, since the energy that leaves as light each second has to come from somewhere.

So the time a star spends on the main sequence, its main-sequence lifetime, is its fuel divided by its luminosity. The Sun's is about 10 billion years. Whether a heavier star lasts longer or shorter depends on how its tank and its burn rate compare, and the next screens measure both.
Use the car idea. The time until the tank is empty is the fuel divided by the rate of burning.

reveal.text: X has more fuel, but it burns it so much faster that it lasts only a quarter as long.

lead.text: Now give the stars different masses. The fuel is the easy part. A star with twice the mass has about twice the hydrogen, so the tank grows in proportion to the mass M, measured in solar masses (M☉).

The burn rate grows far faster. Astronomers have measured the masses and luminosities of many main-sequence stars, and in solar units they follow roughly L = M³·⁵. A star of 3 M☉ shines at about 3³·⁵ = 3³ × √3 = 27 × 1.73 ≈ 47 L☉. The fit is rough, good to about a factor of two, but the steepness is what matters. Tripling the mass multiplies the fuel by 3 and the burn rate by nearly 50.

afterFigure.text: The chart shows the same thing. Moving up the main sequence takes you to heavier stars. The three stars in the picture have about 0.12, 1 and 2 solar masses, and each step up in mass lifts a star far higher on the band.

lead.text: Work it the way the last screen did for 3 M☉: the whole-number part of the power, times a square root for the half.

reveal.text: A 2 M☉ star shines at about 11 L☉, with twice the fuel to feed it. Mass fixes where a main-sequence star sits on the chart.

lead.text: Divide the fuel by the burn rate. The fuel is proportional to M and the burn rate to M³·⁵, so the lifetime is proportional to M ÷ M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵. The exponent is negative because the burn rate grows faster than the fuel, and a negative exponent makes the lifetime shrink as the mass goes up.
Scale the rule to the Sun, whose lifetime is about 10 billion years: t = 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, or 10 billion years ÷ M²·⁵, with M in solar masses. To work out M²·⁵, take M² and multiply it by √M.

Try it on a few masses. A star of 10 M☉ has M²·⁵ ≈ 316, so it lasts about 32 million years. A star with a quarter of the Sun's mass has M⁻²·⁵ = 4²·⁵ = 32, so the rule gives 320 billion years, far longer than the universe has existed. Red dwarfs, the lightest stars, live so long that none has yet run out of fuel.

steps.headline: Find the main-sequence lifetime of a 2 M☉ star.

workedSteps.text: Work out the power of the mass.
Divide the Sun's lifetime by it.
Calculate.

lead.text: Same rule, a heavier star. Give the answer in millions of years.

reveal.text: A star four times the Sun's mass lasts only about 3% as long. More fuel does not make up for a much faster burn.

lead.text: Astronomers can often tell how long a star can last, for instance by dating the cluster it belongs to, and then want its mass. The rule has to run in reverse. Divide the lifetime by 10 billion years to get M⁻²·⁵. Take the reciprocal to get M²·⁵, then raise that to the power 1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.4 to get M.

As an example, take a star that lasts one hundredth as long as the Sun. Then M²·⁵ = 100, and M = 100⁰·⁴ = 10⁰·⁸ ≈ 6.3 solar masses. A calculator does the power in one step with its power key. A short-lived star is a heavy one, and the shorter the life, the heavier the star.
Turn the rule round, step by step, as on the last screen.

reveal.text: A star that lasts only 10 million years is about 16 times the Sun's mass. Short lives mean heavy stars.

lead.text: When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the star's time on the main sequence is over. The core shrinks and heats up while the outer layers swell, and the star leaves the band to become a giant. The Sun will do this in about five billion years.

What happens next depends on the star's mass. A star below about 10 M☉ sheds its outer layers and leaves its core as a white dwarf. A star from about 10 to 40 M☉ ends when its core collapses in a violent explosion called a supernova, and leaves a neutron star, a ball of neutrons about 20 km across with more mass than the Sun. Above about 40 M☉ the collapse leaves a black hole, a region where gravity is so strong that the escape speed is higher than the speed of light.

afterFigure.text: These boundaries are approximate. The figure lists the remnant for three masses, and the mass the star starts with is what decides which it becomes.

lead.text: This star is far heavier than the Sun but not among the heaviest. Use the mass boundaries from the last screen.

reveal.text: A star's initial mass decides its remnant. A 15 M☉ star sits in the middle band: its core collapses in a supernova but stops short of a black hole.

blocks.text: The last lesson ended with a band of stars across the chart, the main sequence, and the fact that a star's mass decides where on the band it sits. Heavy stars blaze at the top left and light ones glow faintly at the bottom right. Mass also decides something else, which is how long a star lasts.

The Sun has shone for about 4.6 billion years and has about as long again to go. A star ten times as heavy does not last anything like that. It burns out in a few tens of millions of years, which is less time than has passed since the dinosaurs died. That looks backwards, because a heavier star has more fuel to burn.

To see why, think of a car's fuel tank. How far a car goes depends on the size of the tank and on how fast the engine drinks. This lesson treats a star the same way: it sets the star's fuel against its thirst, then follows the star to the end of its life.
