recap.nextHook: Stars live and die inside galaxies, vast islands of stars. The next lesson looks at the light of distant galaxies, whose spectral lines are shifted just as a moving star's are.

lessons.title: Galaxies and Hubble's law

lead.text: A galaxy is a great gathering of stars held together by gravity. Our own, the Milky Way, holds a few hundred billion stars, and the faint smudges that telescopes find all over the sky are other galaxies of the same kind. They lie far beyond the stars of our own sky, so far that even the parsec is too small a unit. Astronomers use the megaparsec (Mpc), a million parsecs, which is 3.26 million light-years.

A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, so a distance in light-years is also a time. Light from an object 100 light-years away has been on its way for 100 years. The Large Magellanic Cloud, a small neighbouring galaxy 0.05 Mpc away, lies 0.05 × 3.26 million = 163,000 light-years off, and we see it as it was 163,000 years ago.
Distance and the age of the light go together. The farther away a galaxy is, the longer ago the light we see left it, so a telescope looks back in time as well as out in space.
Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy. Turn its distance into the travel time of its light.

reveal.text: You were looking at Andromeda as it was millions of years ago. The farther away a galaxy is, the older the light we see.

lead.text: Now the spectra. The lines in a galaxy's light are shifted to the red, and each shift gives a speed through the rule from the lesson on colour and motion, v = c × Δλ/λ. Here Δλ/λ is the stretch of a line as a fraction of its original wavelength, and c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s is the speed of light. A galaxy whose lines are stretched by 1% is receding at 3,000 km/s.

Hubble compared those speeds with the distances to the same galaxies and found that they rise together. Hubble's law says v = H₀ × d, where d is the distance. The constant H₀, the Hubble constant, is about 70 km/s per Mpc. For every megaparsec of distance a galaxy recedes 70 km/s faster, so a galaxy 10 Mpc away recedes at 700 km/s and one 20 Mpc away at 1,400 km/s.

afterFigure.text: The two galaxies in the picture obey the same law. Their points lie on a straight line through the origin of the graph, so twice the distance means twice the speed. The Mpc in H₀ cancels the Mpc in d, which leaves the speed in km/s.

steps.headline: How fast does a galaxy 30 Mpc away recede, with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc?

workedSteps.text: Use Hubble's law.
Put in the numbers. The Mpc cancels.
Calculate.

lead.text: Same law, a farther galaxy. Remember H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc.

reveal.text: Twice the distance gives twice the speed. At 200 Mpc the same law gives double what you just found.

lead.text: Why should speed rise with distance? A rubber sheet gives a picture. Mark dots on it in a straight line, with dot B 5 cm from dot A and dot C 15 cm from A. Now stretch the sheet evenly until every gap is 20% longer. B's gap grows from 5 cm to 6 cm, a gain of 1 cm. C's gap grows from 15 cm to 18 cm, a gain of 3 cm.

Evenly means every gap grows by the same fraction of its own length, so a gap three times as long gains three times as much. The stretching takes the same time for both, so the farther dot moves away three times as fast. That is Hubble's law, with the dots as galaxies: the farther the galaxy, the faster it recedes.

The picture also changes how to think about the galaxies. They do not need to be flying through space like fragments from a blast. The space between them can stretch, and the galaxies are carried apart with it.
Use the stretching sheet. Every gap grows by the same fraction of its own length.

reveal.text: Each gap gains its own length, so the longer gap gains more. That is why speed rises with distance.

lead.text: Go back to the sheet and stand on any dot. Every other dot moves away from you, and the dots farther from you move away faster, whichever dot you stand on. Nothing on the sheet marks a centre, and each dot sees the pattern Hubble found.

That answers the worry that we sit at the centre of an explosion. We see galaxies receding in every direction because the whole universe is stretching, and an astronomer in the Andromeda galaxy would see the Milky Way and the rest moving away from her in just the same way. Hubble's law follows from the even stretching, so it holds from every galaxy.
Hubble's law can be turned round to give a distance. A galaxy too far for parallax still has a redshift, and once the redshift has given the speed, the distance is d = v ÷ H₀.
Here is the whole chain for one galaxy. A line that should lie at 400.0 nm is seen at 404.0 nm. The stretch is 4.0/400.0 = 0.01, so v = 3.00 × 10⁵ × 0.01 = 3,000 km/s. Then d = 3,000 ÷ 70 ≈ 43 Mpc.

afterFigure.text: The value of H₀ is not known exactly. Different methods give values between about 67 and 73 km/s per Mpc, and the disagreement is called the Hubble tension. Every distance found this way is divided by H₀, so each inherits that uncertainty.

lead.text: A recession speed gives a distance by d = v ÷ H₀, with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc.

reveal.text: A faster galaxy is a farther one: you have turned a measured speed into a distance.

lead.text: Two estimates of H₀ give two different speeds for the same galaxy, and the gap between them depends on how far away it is.

reveal.text: The two values predict speeds that differ by the gap in H₀ times the distance. A small disagreement in H₀ grows with distance.

blocks.text: Stars live and die inside galaxies, and a galaxy's light has spectral lines just as a single star's does. Measure those lines in almost any galaxy and they have moved towards the red. Last time a redshift meant one thing, that the source is moving away, so nearly every galaxy in the sky must be moving away from us.

In 1929 Edwin Hubble set those motions beside the distances to the galaxies and found a pattern. The farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is going. That looks like an explosion with us at the centre, yet an astronomer in any other galaxy would see the same pattern and could say the same about their own position.

This lesson retraces the discovery. It starts with how far away galaxies are, then sets out the pattern, explains with a stretching sheet why it has no centre, and ends by using it to find the distances to galaxies too far for parallax.

recap.keyIdea: Galaxies recede at v = H₀d, so a redshift gives a distance. Uniform expansion looks the same from every galaxy, so it has no centre.

blocks.text: You began with the pattern Hubble found and traced it to a stretching sheet. A galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at 7,000 km/s, a galaxy receding at 14,000 km/s is 200 Mpc away, and the sheet gives every galaxy the same view.

recap.nextHook: If every galaxy is moving apart, they were all once close together. The next lesson runs the expansion backwards to find when that was, and looks for the glow such a beginning would leave.

lessons.title: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang

lead.text: Distance divided by speed gives a time. A car now 60 km from your door and driving away at a steady 40 km/h set off 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 hours ago, as long as it has kept the same speed all the way.

The same reasoning works on a galaxy. If it has always moved at its present speed, a galaxy at distance d moving at speed v set off d ÷ v ago. Hubble's law says v = H₀d, so the time is d ÷ (H₀d). The distance cancels and the time is 1/H₀, whatever the galaxy.

Every galaxy gives the same answer, because a galaxy twice as far away is moving twice as fast and the two doublings cancel. All of them set off from the same place at the same moment. The time since then, 1/H₀, is called the expansion age.
The time since setting off is the distance travelled divided by the speed.

reveal.text: A steady speed gives time = distance ÷ speed, the same reasoning that dates the expansion.

lead.text: The value 1/H₀ is a time, but H₀ is quoted in km/s per Mpc, so the units need tidying before it reads as years. Write 1 Mpc as 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km. Then H₀ is a number of km/s per 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km, and the kilometres cancel in 1/H₀, which leaves seconds.

Divide 3.086 × 10¹⁹ by the value of H₀ to get seconds. Then divide by the number of seconds in a billion years, 3.156 × 10¹⁶, to get billions of years. The next example does it for H₀ = 60 km/s per Mpc.
Working both conversions through once gives a shortcut for later: 1/H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀, with H₀ in km/s per Mpc.

steps.headline: Find 1/H₀ in billions of years for H₀ = 60 km/s per Mpc.

workedSteps.text: Write 1 Mpc in kilometres, so the kilometres cancel.
Divide to get seconds.
Divide by the seconds in a billion years.

lead.text: Same method with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc. Use 1 Mpc = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km and 1 billion years = 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s.

reveal.text: About 14 billion years. Careful modelling of the changing expansion gives 13.8 billion years, so this simple estimate is close.

lead.text: The answer is rough, because it assumes each galaxy has always moved at its present speed. The expansion has not been steady. Gravity pulled on everything and slowed the expansion in the early universe, and later an effect called dark energy made it speed up again. The slowing and the speeding up nearly cancel, so 1/H₀ lands close to the age that careful modelling gives, 13.8 billion years.

The estimate also depends on the value of H₀. A smaller H₀ means slower expansion, so the galaxies took longer to reach their present positions. With the shortcut 1/H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀, H₀ = 90 gives 10.9 billion years, and a smaller H₀ gives a longer time.
Use 1/H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀, which has the unit conversion built in.

reveal.text: At H₀ = 50 the universe would be older, 19.6 billion years. A slower expansion needs longer to reach the same spread.

lead.text: If the galaxies were once squeezed together, the early universe was dense and extremely hot, and hot things glow. For its first few hundred thousand years it was a glowing fog of charged particles, and light could not travel far before colliding with them.

As the universe expanded it cooled. About 380,000 years after the beginning it had fallen to roughly 3,000 K, cool enough for electrons and nuclei to join into neutral atoms. The fog cleared and light could cross space freely. Some of that light has been travelling ever since, so it should fill the sky today.

In 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, working with a radio antenna in New Jersey, picked up a faint microwave signal that came equally from every direction. It is called the cosmic microwave background. Its spectrum is a blackbody at 2.725 K, the closest match to a perfect thermal spectrum ever measured.
Wien's law applies as before: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T. Give the answer in millimetres.

reveal.text: A peak near a millimetre lies in the microwave range, which is how the background got its name.

lead.text: The glow left at about 3,000 K but arrives at 2.725 K. The difference comes from the expansion. While the light crossed space, space stretched, and the waves stretched with it, in the same way a redshift stretches a galaxy's spectral lines. The stretch applies to every wavelength alike, so the whole spectrum slides to longer wavelengths and keeps its blackbody shape.

Wien's law links the two changes. The peak wavelength is inversely proportional to the temperature, so if every wavelength grows 100 times, the peak is 100 times longer and the temperature is 100 times lower. The figure shows a glow at 300 K and the same glow stretched 100 times.

afterFigure.text: So the stretch factor is the earlier temperature divided by the later one, and a single wavelength grows by the same factor. Light that left as visible or infrared light arrives as microwaves.

cases.label: The same glow stretched 100 times, 3 K

lead.text: The glow was released at about 3,000 K and is now at 2.725 K. Compare the two temperatures.

reveal.text: Every wavelength has grown about a thousand-fold. Glow that left as visible and infrared light now arrives as microwaves.

blocks.text: Hubble's pattern says every galaxy is moving away from every other, and the farther apart they are, the faster. Run a film of that backwards and the galaxies drift together. At some moment in the film they all arrive in the same place.

That moment is the Big Bang, and the film also says how long ago it was. It says something about the early universe as well. Squeezed into a small space, everything was dense and hot. If the universe was once that hot, some of its light should still be crossing space today, much cooled.

This lesson dates the beginning from the expansion rate, using nothing more than distance divided by speed. Then it looks for the afterglow, a faint light found by accident in 1965, and uses Wien's law once more to read what it has become.

questions.prompt: Amsterdam is at latitude 52° N. What is the altitude of the north celestial pole there, in degrees?
hints: Compare the two ends of the walk: at each, what is the latitude and what is the pole’s altitude?
At both ends the pole’s altitude has the same value as the latitude.
If that stays true all the way along, what is the altitude at Amsterdam’s latitude?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pole’s altitude equals the latitude: 52°.

questions.onCorrect: 52°. The pole stands as high above the horizon as your latitude. The next screen shows why.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the pole’s altitude at the North Pole, latitude 90°. Amsterdam is much further south.
That is 90° minus the latitude, the angle between the pole and the point straight overhead. The question asks for the angle above the horizon.

questions.prompt: The sky turns about 15° an hour. Through what angle, in degrees, does a star move around its daily circle in 6 hours?
hints: The rate is constant through the night.
Multiply the rate by the time.
Calculate 15 × 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 15° per hour × 6 h = 90°, a quarter of a full circle.

questions.onCorrect: 90°. Steady turning means angle = rate × time, so 6 hours is a quarter of a circle.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the hours to the rate. They are different quantities: multiply them instead.
That divides the rate by the hours. The angle grows with time, so the hours multiply.

questions.prompt: From latitude 52° N, a star is circumpolar when its declination exceeds 90° − φ. What is that smallest declination, in degrees?
hints: The lowest point of the star's circle must stay above the horizon.
The lowest point lies 90° − δ below a pole that is φ high.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ > 90° − 52° = 38°. Stars north of +38° never set from 52° N.

questions.onCorrect: 38°. The limit is measured from the pole, so subtract the latitude from 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude itself. The limit is measured from the pole, so the latitude has to be taken from 90°.
Only a star exactly at the pole would qualify under that limit. Every star close to it must qualify as well.

questions.prompt: A star of declination +20° crosses the meridian as seen from latitude 52° N. What is its altitude then, in degrees?
hints: The highest altitude comes on the meridian.
Find the difference between latitude and declination, then subtract it from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: 58°. Altitude on the meridian is 90° minus the gap between latitude and declination.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. The altitude is what is left of 90° after the gap.
That adds latitude and declination. The rule uses the difference between them.

questions.prompt: Seen from latitude 30° N, a star of declination −10° crosses the meridian. Find its altitude in degrees.
hints: A southern declination enters with a minus sign.
The difference φ − δ is 30 − (−10).
Subtract that difference from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: 50°. A southern declination keeps its minus sign, so the gap is 40° and the altitude is 90° minus it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. Take it away from 90°.
That treats −10° as +10°. A southern declination keeps its sign, which makes the gap larger.

questions.prompt: What single word names a star that never sets as seen from a given latitude?
hints: The star's circle stays around the pole without dipping below the horizon.

acceptedIdeas: circumpolar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Circumpolar: its whole daily circle stays above the horizon around the celestial pole.

questions.onCorrect: Circumpolar: the whole daily circle stays above the horizon.

misconceptions.feedback: The meridian is a line across the sky, not a kind of star. The word you want describes a star that never sets.

questions.prompt: London lies at 51.5° N. Taking Earth's tilt as 23.4°, find the Sun's noon altitude at the June solstice, in degrees, to one decimal place.
hints: At the June solstice the Sun's declination equals the tilt, north of the equator.
Find 51.5 − 23.4 first, then subtract it from 90.
questions.onCorrect: 61.9°. The June Sun's declination is +23.4°, which narrows the gap to London's latitude.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. The altitude is what is left of 90° after the gap.
That is the December figure. In June the Sun is north of the equator, so the gap is smaller.

questions.prompt: Find the Sun's noon altitude in London (51.5° N) at the December solstice, with a tilt of 23.4°, to one decimal place.
hints: In December the Sun's declination is south of the equator, so it is negative.
Subtract that sum from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the December solstice δ = −23.4°. Altitude = 90° − |51.5° + 23.4°| = 90° − 74.9° = 15.1°.

questions.onCorrect: 15.1°. In December the Sun's declination is −23.4°, so the gap to London grows and the Sun stays low.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the June figure. In December the declination is negative and the gap grows.
That is the gap between latitude and declination. Take it away from 90°.

questions.prompt: At an equinox the Sun's declination is 0°. Find the noon altitude of the Sun from latitude 40° N, in degrees.
hints: Set δ to zero.
The rule reduces to 90° − φ.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: 50°. At an equinox δ is 0°, so the noon altitude is simply 90° minus the latitude.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude. Altitude is measured up from the horizon, so take the latitude away from 90°.

questions.prompt: Imagine Earth had no axial tilt. What would the Sun's noon altitude be in London (51.5° N) on every date, in degrees, to one decimal place?
hints: Without tilt the Sun never leaves the celestial equator.
Its declination is zero on every date.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no tilt δ = 0° all year, so the noon altitude is always 90° − 51.5° = 38.5°.

questions.onCorrect: 38.5°. With no tilt δ stays 0°, so the noon Sun never changes height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude. Take it away from 90° to get the altitude.
That is London's June figure. With no tilt the Sun never leaves the celestial equator.

questions.prompt: At what northern latitude, in degrees, is the noon Sun directly overhead at the June solstice, taking Earth's tilt as 23.4°? Give one decimal place.
hints: Directly overhead means an altitude of 90°.
Set 90° − |φ − δ| equal to 90°.
The latitude must match the Sun's declination on that date.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Overhead means altitude 90°, so |φ − δ| = 0 and φ = δ = 23.4° N, the Tropic of Cancer.

questions.onCorrect: 23.4° N. The Sun is overhead where latitude equals its declination, the Tropic of Cancer in June.

misconceptions.feedback: 90° is the Sun's altitude, not a latitude. The question asks where on Earth that happens.
The equator sees the overhead Sun at the equinoxes. At the June solstice the Sun is north of it.

questions.prompt: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Why is it winter in the northern hemisphere then?
hints: Compare the two hemispheres: they have opposite seasons at the same distance from the Sun.

acceptedIdeas: The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so sunlight arrives low and days are short
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Seasons follow the tilt. In January the north leans away from the Sun: a low noon Sun spreads its energy thinly over short days, while the 3% change in distance matters little.

choices.label: The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so sunlight arrives low and days are short
The Sun gives out less energy in January
Earth's orbit carries it farthest from the Sun in January

questions.onCorrect: Seasons follow the tilt. In January the north leans away, so the Sun is low and the days are short.

misconceptions.feedback: The Sun's output hardly changes through the year. The tilt does the work.
The question says Earth is closest in January. Distance cannot explain winter then.

questions.prompt: When the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 90°, what percentage of the Moon's visible disc is lit?
hints: Use lit fraction = (1 − cos θ)/2.
The cosine of 90° is zero.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lit fraction = (1 − cos 90°)/2 = (1 − 0)/2, half the disc.

questions.onCorrect: 50%. At θ = 90° half the disc is lit: the quarter phases show half a disc.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole disc, which happens at θ = 180°. Halfway round, the lit half is only partly turned towards us.
That is the lit fraction at θ = 60°. By 90° more of the lit half has turned towards us.

questions.prompt: The synodic month is 29.53 days. How many degrees per day does the Moon gain on the Sun? Give one decimal place.
hints: In one synodic month the Moon gains one full turn on the Sun.
A full turn is 360°.
Divide 360 by the number of days.
questions.onCorrect: 12.2° a day. One full turn spread steadily over the synodic month.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole turn. The question asks how much is gained each day.
That is the number of days. Share the full turn out over them.

questions.prompt: At which phase of the Moon can a lunar eclipse happen? Answer with one word.
hints: Earth's shadow points directly away from the Sun.

acceptedIdeas: full
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Full: Earth must sit between the Sun and the Moon so the Moon can pass through Earth's shadow.

questions.onCorrect: Full: Earth must sit between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon can enter Earth's shadow.

misconceptions.feedback: At new moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun. Earth's shadow points away from the Sun, so the Moon would have to be on the far side.

questions.prompt: The Moon is 3,475 km across and 384,400 km away. Find its angular diameter in degrees, to two decimal places, using angle ≈ diameter/distance and 1 radian = 57.3°.
hints: Divide the diameter by the distance to get radians.
Convert radians to degrees with the factor 57.3.
Round the result to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: 0.52°. Angular size is diameter ÷ distance in radians, times 57.3 for degrees.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the angle in radians. Multiply by 57.3 to turn it into degrees.

questions.prompt: How many days after new moon is first quarter, taking the synodic month as 29.53 days? Give two decimal places.
hints: First quarter is a Sun–Earth–Moon angle of 90°.
That is one quarter of the full cycle.
Divide the synodic month by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First quarter is a quarter of the cycle: 29.53 ÷ 4 = 7.3825, about 7.38 days.

questions.onCorrect: 7.38 days. First quarter is θ = 90°, a quarter of the way round the cycle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is half the cycle, the full moon. First quarter comes a quarter of the way round.
That is three quarters of the cycle: third quarter. First quarter comes earlier.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the Moon's visible disc is lit when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 120°?
hints: Use (1 − cos θ)/2.
The cosine of 120° is −0.5.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 75%. At θ = 120° the cosine is negative, so more than half the disc is lit.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats cos 120° as +0.5. It is negative, which makes the lit part larger.
That would be θ = 90°. At 120° more of the lit half has turned towards us.

questions.prompt: An asteroid's orbit has semi-major axis 2 AU and eccentricity 0.6. How close does it come to the Sun, in AU?
hints: The Sun sits at a focus, a × e from the centre.
Perihelion distance is a(1 − e).
Calculate 2 × (1 − 0.6).
questions.onCorrect: 0.8 AU. The Sun sits a × e from the centre, so perihelion is a(1 − e).

misconceptions.feedback: That is a × e, the gap between the Sun and the centre. Closest approach is measured from the Sun, so take that gap off a.
That is the far end. The closest point lies on the near side of the Sun.

questions.prompt: For the orbit with a = 2 AU and e = 0.6, the speed at perihelion divided by the speed at aphelion equals the aphelion distance divided by the perihelion distance. Find this ratio.
hints: Aphelion is a(1 + e) and perihelion is a(1 − e).
Work out both distances.
Divide 3.2 by 0.8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Aphelion 3.2 AU ÷ perihelion 0.8 AU = 4. The asteroid moves four times faster at its closest point.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The speeds are in the inverse ratio of the distances, so the closer end is faster.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. The planet is faster at the closer end.
That is the aphelion distance, not a ratio of the two distances.

questions.prompt: An asteroid orbits the Sun with semi-major axis 4 AU. Using P² = a³ (P in years, a in AU), find its period in years.
hints: Cube the semi-major axis.
That gives P².
Take the square root of 64.
questions.onCorrect: 8 years. Cube a to get P², then take the square root.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P². The law gives the square of the period, so take the square root.
That is the square root of a. The law cubes a first.

questions.prompt: A planet orbits a star of 4 solar masses with a = 1 AU. Using P² = a³/M, find its period in years.
hints: Divide a³ by the star's mass in solar masses.
1 cubed is 1.
Take the square root of a quarter.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5 years. A heavier star divides P² by M, so the period shrinks.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P². Take the square root to get the period.
That is the period around a Sun-like star. A heavier star pulls harder and shortens it.

questions.prompt: Jupiter's orbital period is 11.86 years. Using P² = a³, find its semi-major axis in AU, to two decimal places.
hints: Square the period to get a³.
11.86² is about 140.7.
Take the cube root of that.
questions.onCorrect: 5.20 AU. Square the period to get a³, then take the cube root.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a³. Take the cube root to find a.
That is the square root of the period. P² = a³ makes a the cube root of P².

questions.prompt: What name is given to the point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun?
hints: It begins with the Greek prefix for 'near'.

acceptedIdeas: perihelion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Perihelion, from Greek peri (near) and helios (Sun). The farthest point is aphelion.

questions.onCorrect: Perihelion: peri means near and helios means Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: Aphelion is the farthest point. The closest point has the prefix that means near.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 3r. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change? Give three decimal places.
hints: Gravity follows an inverse-square law.
Square the factor by which the distance grew.
Take the reciprocal of 3².
questions.onCorrect: 0.111. Force follows 1/r², so tripling the separation divides the force by nine.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the force as falling in proportion to the distance. Gravity follows the square of it.
That makes the force grow. The force weakens as the bodies move apart.

questions.prompt: At a fixed separation, one mass is doubled and the other tripled. By what factor does the gravitational force change?
hints: The force is proportional to the product of the masses.
Each mass change multiplies the force.
Multiply the two factors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ Mm, so the force changes by 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Force is proportional to the product of the masses, so the factors multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the factors. The force depends on the product of the masses, so the factors multiply.

questions.prompt: Earth's GM is 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and its radius is 6,371 km. Find g = GM/R² at the surface, in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Convert the radius to metres first.
Square 6.371 × 10⁶ m.
Divide GM by that square.
questions.onCorrect: 9.82 m/s². Surface gravity is GM divided by the radius squared, in metres.

misconceptions.feedback: The radius must be in metres to match GM. In kilometres the answer comes out a million times too large.

questions.prompt: How many times as large as the Moon's pull on Earth is Earth's pull on the Moon?
hints: Think of the pair as a tug of war between two bodies.
Whatever force acts on one body from the other, the other feels a force from it.
Newton's third law pairs the two forces.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both forces equal GMm/r², so the ratio is exactly one: equal and opposite.

questions.onCorrect: 1. The two forces are an equal and opposite pair: GMm/r² is the same whichever body you call M.

misconceptions.feedback: The 81 shows up in how much each body accelerates, not in the size of the pull. Think of the pair as one tug of war.

questions.prompt: Mars has GM = 4.283 × 10¹³ m³/s² and radius 3,390 km. Find its surface gravity in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Use g = GM/R² with R in metres.
Square 3.39 × 10⁶.
Divide GM by that square.
questions.onCorrect: 3.73 m/s². The same formula gives each world's surface gravity from its own GM and radius.

misconceptions.feedback: The radius must be in metres to match GM. Kilometres give an answer a million times too large.

questions.prompt: Why do a hammer and a feather dropped together on the Moon land together?
hints: Divide the gravitational force by the falling object's own mass.

acceptedIdeas: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Force GMm/r² divided by the object's mass m leaves GM/r², the same for any object at that place. With no air there is no drag to separate them.

choices.label: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
The Moon's gravity does not act on light objects
Heavier objects are pulled less strongly per kilogram

questions.onCorrect: The mass cancels in GMm/r² ÷ m, leaving GM/r². The acceleration is the same for every object.

misconceptions.feedback: Gravity acts on light and heavy objects alike. The question is what it does to their acceleration.
Divide GMm/r² by m and see whether any of the object's own mass is left.

questions.prompt: Find the circular orbital speed 400 km above Earth, where r = 6,771 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Use v = √(GM/r) with r in metres.
Divide GM by 6.771 × 10⁶ m.
Take the square root and convert from m/s to km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 7.67 km/s. Divide GM by r in metres, take the square root, then convert to km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 to give km/s.

questions.prompt: Find the escape speed from Earth's surface, with R = 6,371 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Use v = √(2GM/r).
Double GM, then divide by the radius in metres.
Take the square root and convert to km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 11.19 km/s. The escape speed has a 2 under the root, so it exceeds the circular speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the circular speed at the surface. Escape needs more, with the extra 2 under the root.
That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 for km/s.

questions.prompt: Using v = √(GM/r) with GM☉ = 1.327 × 10²⁰ m³/s² and r = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, find Earth's orbital speed in km/s, to one decimal place.
hints: This is a circular-orbit speed around the Sun.
Divide GM☉ by the distance in metres.
Take the square root, then divide by 1,000.
questions.onCorrect: 29.8 km/s. The same circular-speed formula works around the Sun with the Sun's GM.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 for km/s.

questions.prompt: Tidal stretching falls as the cube of distance. If the Moon were at half its present distance, by what factor would its tides grow?
hints: A tide is a difference in pull across Earth.
That difference scales as one over distance cubed.
Cube the factor of 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tide ∝ 1/d³, so halving d multiplies the tide by 2³ = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. A tide is a difference in pull, which scales as 1/d³, so half the distance gives 2³.

misconceptions.feedback: That squares the factor, as for the pull itself. A tide is a difference in pull, which follows the cube.
That follows 1/d. The difference in pull falls faster, as 1/d³.

questions.prompt: The Moon has GM = 4.90 × 10¹² m³/s² and radius 1,737 km. Find the escape speed from its surface in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Escape speed is √(2GM/R).
Convert the radius to metres.
Compute the square root and convert to km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 2.38 km/s. Escape speed is √(2GM/R) with the radius in metres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the circular speed at the surface. The escape speed is larger, with a 2 under the root.

questions.prompt: Why are the tides largest around new moon and full moon?
hints: Think about where the Sun lies relative to the Earth–Moon line at those phases.

acceptedIdeas: The Sun's and the Moon's tidal stretches line up and add
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are in line, so the solar tide (0.46 of the lunar tide) adds to the Moon's: spring tides. At the quarters they partly cancel: neap tides.

choices.label: The Sun's and the Moon's tidal stretches line up and add
The Moon is always closest to Earth at those phases
Earth spins faster at those phases

questions.onCorrect: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon line up, so the two tidal stretches add.

misconceptions.feedback: The Moon's distance varies over the month, but not in step with the phase.
Earth's spin does not change with the Moon's phase. Look at how the Sun and Moon line up.

questions.prompt: A probe moves from 1 AU to 2 AU from the Sun. What fraction of the solar flux it received at 1 AU does it now receive?
hints: Light spreads over a sphere of area 4πd².
Doubling d multiplies that area by 2².
Take the reciprocal of 2².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Flux ∝ 1/d², so it falls to 1/2² = 1/4 = 0.25 of its value at 1 AU.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25. Flux follows 1/d², so doubling the distance divides the flux by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves the flux. It follows the inverse square, so the 2 is squared.
That makes the flux grow. It weakens as the star gets farther.

questions.prompt: The Sun's luminosity is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W. Find the flux at 1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, in W/m², to the nearest whole number.
hints: Use F = L/(4πd²).
Square the distance in metres, then multiply by 4π.
Divide the luminosity by that area.
questions.onCorrect: 1,361 W/m². Divide the luminosity by the sphere's area, 4πd² in metres.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the 4π. The light spreads over a whole sphere of area 4πd².

questions.prompt: Proxima Centauri's parallax is 0.768 arcseconds. Find its distance in parsecs, to two decimal places.
hints: Distance in parsecs is the reciprocal of parallax in arcseconds.
Divide 1 by the parallax.
Round to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: 1.30 pc. Distance in parsecs is the reciprocal of parallax in arcseconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the parallax itself. The distance is its reciprocal.

questions.prompt: Star A is 100 times as luminous as star B, yet they appear equally bright. How many times farther away than B is A?
hints: Flux is proportional to L/d².
Keep the flux fixed while L grows a hundredfold.
Then d² must grow by the same factor; take the square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal flux needs L/d² equal, so d grows as √L: √100 = 10 times farther.

questions.onCorrect: 10 times. Equal flux needs L/d² fixed, so d grows as the square root of L.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the luminosity factor. Flux falls as 1/d², so the distance grows only as its square root.
That squares the factor. The distance must grow as the square root of the luminosity.

questions.prompt: A star's parallax is 0.05 arcseconds. Find its distance in light-years, to one decimal place, using 1 pc = 3.26 ly.
hints: First convert parallax to parsecs with d = 1/p.
Then multiply by 3.26 light-years per parsec.
questions.onCorrect: 65.2 ly. Take the reciprocal of the parallax for parsecs, then multiply by 3.26.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance in parsecs. Convert to light-years with 3.26.
That multiplies the parallax by 3.26. Take the reciprocal of the parallax first.

questions.prompt: What unit of distance is defined as the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond?
hints: Its name joins the first syllables of the two words that define it.

acceptedIdeas: parsec
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The parsec: PARallax of one arcSECond. It equals 206,265 AU or 3.26 light-years.

questions.onCorrect: The parsec: the distance at which the parallax is one arcsecond.

misconceptions.feedback: A light-year is a distance too, but light's travel in a year defines it. Parallax defines the unit you want.

questions.prompt: Using Wien's law λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find the peak wavelength of the Sun (T = 5,772 K) in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Divide Wien's constant by the temperature.
The result comes out in metres.
Multiply by 10⁹ to convert metres to nanometres.
questions.onCorrect: 502 nm. Wien's law gives metres; multiply by 10⁹ to get nanometres.

questions.prompt: A star's spectrum peaks at 290 nm. Find its surface temperature in kelvin, to the nearest hundred.
hints: Rearrange Wien's law for T.
Write the peak wavelength in metres.
Divide the constant by that wavelength, then round.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 9,993 K, which is 10,000 K to the nearest hundred.

questions.onCorrect: 10,000 K. Divide the constant by the peak wavelength in metres, then round.

misconceptions.feedback: Round your answer to the nearest hundred, as the question asks.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen line with laboratory wavelength 656.28 nm is observed at 662.84 nm. Using v = cΔλ/λ with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, find the radial velocity in km/s, to the nearest ten (positive means receding).
hints: Find the shift: observed minus laboratory wavelength.
Divide the shift by the laboratory wavelength.
Multiply by the speed of light in km/s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Δλ = 6.56 nm; v = 3.00 × 10⁵ × 6.56/656.28 = 2,999 km/s, which is 3,000 km/s to the nearest ten, receding.

questions.onCorrect: 3,000 km/s receding. Shift ÷ laboratory wavelength × c gives the speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shift in nanometres. Divide by the laboratory wavelength, then multiply by c.
The line moved to a longer wavelength. That is a redshift, so the velocity is positive.

questions.prompt: A star approaches at 150 km/s. Find the shift of its 500.00 nm line in nanometres, with redshift positive and blueshift negative, to three decimal places. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s.
hints: An approaching source has a negative radial velocity.
Use Δλ = λv/c.
Multiply 500 by −150, then divide by 300,000.
questions.onCorrect: −0.25 nm. An approaching star has negative velocity, so its lines shift towards the blue.

misconceptions.feedback: The star is approaching, so the line moves to shorter wavelengths. That makes the shift negative.

questions.prompt: Betelgeuse looks orange-red and Rigel looks blue-white. What does the difference tell you?
hints: Which property of a glowing body sets where its spectrum peaks?

acceptedIdeas: Betelgeuse's surface is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Colour tracks surface temperature through Wien's law: about 3,600 K for Betelgeuse against about 12,000 K for Rigel. Their radial speeds are far too small to change a colour.

choices.label: Betelgeuse's surface is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
Betelgeuse is moving away from us much faster than Rigel
Betelgeuse is farther away, so its light has reddened on the way

questions.onCorrect: Colour tracks surface temperature through Wien's law: orange-red is cooler, blue-white hotter.

misconceptions.feedback: A speed of a few km/s shifts a line by a tiny fraction. It cannot change a star's colour.
These bright stars are near enough that reddening on the way is small. The colour is set at the surface.

questions.prompt: A red dwarf has a surface temperature of 3,000 K. Find its peak wavelength in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Use λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T.
Divide by 3,000 K.
Convert metres to nanometres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 3,000 = 9.66 × 10⁻⁷ m = 966 nm, in the near infrared.

questions.onCorrect: 966 nm, in the near infrared. A cool star peaks at long wavelengths.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres. Multiply by 10⁹ to turn it into nanometres.

questions.prompt: A star has the Sun's radius but twice the Sun's surface temperature. How many times the Sun's luminosity does it emit?
hints: Use L = R²(T/T☉)⁴ in solar units.
The radius factor is one.
Raise the temperature ratio to the fourth power.
questions.onCorrect: 16. Luminosity goes as T⁴, so doubling the temperature multiplies it by 2⁴.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats luminosity as proportional to T². It follows the fourth power.
That doubles the luminosity with the temperature. Each square metre emits power proportional to T⁴.
That is 2³. The power per square metre goes as T⁴.

questions.prompt: A red supergiant has a surface temperature of 3,600 K and a radius of 760 R☉. With T☉ = 5,772 K, find its luminosity in solar units, to the nearest thousand.
hints: Square the radius in solar radii.
Raise 3,600/5,772 to the fourth power.
Multiply the two results, then round.
questions.onCorrect: 87,000 L☉. The huge R² outweighs the cool surface's small T⁴ factor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is R² alone. Multiply it by the temperature factor (T/T☉)⁴ as well.
That is the temperature factor alone. Multiply it by R² too.

questions.prompt: A white dwarf has radius 0.01 R☉ and a surface temperature four times the Sun's. Find its luminosity in solar units, to four decimal places.
hints: Square the radius.
Raise the temperature factor to the fourth power.
Multiply 0.0001 by 256.
questions.onCorrect: 0.0256 L☉. A tiny R² beats a hot T⁴: hot but dim.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the radius factor alone. Multiply by the temperature factor as well.
That is the temperature factor alone. Multiply by R² as well.

questions.prompt: Two stars have the same surface temperature, but one is far more luminous. Which property of the luminous star must be larger? Answer in one word.
hints: Write L = 4πR²σT⁴ and hold T fixed.

acceptedIdeas: radius
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its radius. Equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so more luminosity needs more surface area.

questions.onCorrect: Radius: equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so more luminosity needs more surface.

misconceptions.feedback: Both stars share the same temperature, so temperature is not what differs. Think about the surface area.

questions.prompt: Two stars have equal temperatures; one is 100 times as luminous as the other. How many times larger is its radius?
hints: Hold T constant in L ∝ R²T⁴.
Luminosity then scales as radius squared.
Take the square root of the luminosity ratio.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With T fixed, L ∝ R², so R grows as √100 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10 times. At fixed T, L ∝ R², so the radius grows as the square root of L.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the luminosity ratio. L goes as R², so the radius ratio is its square root.
That squares the ratio. The radius ratio is the square root of the luminosity ratio.

questions.prompt: A star twice the Sun's radius has a luminosity of 4 L☉. Taking T☉ = 5,772 K, find its surface temperature in kelvin.
hints: Write L = R²(T/T☉)⁴ and substitute R = 2.
Divide both sides by R².
Find what temperature ratio raised to the fourth power gives the result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 = 2² × (T/T☉)⁴ gives (T/T☉)⁴ = 1, so T equals the Sun's temperature: 5,772 K.

questions.onCorrect: 5,772 K. Divide L by R² first, then take the fourth root of what is left.

Equal areas in equal times needs the speed to change as the distance does.

questions.prompt: A comet has perihelion 0.5 AU and aphelion 7.5 AU. Find its semi-major axis, in AU.
hints: The long axis runs from the near end to the far end through the Sun.
Add the two distances to get the long axis.
a is half the long axis.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The long axis is 0.5 + 7.5 = 8 AU, and a is half of it: 4 AU.

questions.onCorrect: 4 AU. The semi-major axis is half the sum of the closest and farthest distances.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole long axis. The semi-major axis is half of it.
That is the difference of the two distances. The long axis is their sum.

questions.prompt: A full cycle from one new moon to the next takes about 30 days. How many days pass between a new moon and the next full moon?
hints: New moon to new moon is the whole cycle.
Full moon sits opposite the Sun, halfway round.
Halve the 30 days.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Full moon is halfway through the cycle: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 days.

questions.onCorrect: 15 days. Full moon comes halfway through the cycle, opposite the Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole cycle, new moon to new moon. Full moon comes part-way through.
That is a quarter of the cycle, first quarter. Full moon comes later.

questions.prompt: Which angle θ between Sun and Moon gives a new moon?
hints: At new moon, none of the lit half faces us.
questions.onCorrect: At θ = 0° the Moon is in line with the Sun and we see only its dark side.

misconceptions.feedback: At 90° half the disc is lit: a quarter phase, not new.
At 180° the Moon is opposite the Sun and fully lit: full moon.

questions.prompt: Why is more than half the disc lit when θ = 150°?
hints: What happens to the lit half as θ grows past 90°?

acceptedIdeas: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.

choices.label: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.
The Moon is closer to Earth then.
The Sun shines more brightly then.

questions.onCorrect: Past 90°, the lit half is turned more towards us than away, so more than half the disc shows.

misconceptions.feedback: Distance does not set the phase. The angle does.
The Sun's brightness does not change. What changes is how much of the lit half we face.

questions.prompt: After one synodic month, what does the Moon show?
hints: The synodic month is the time from one new moon to the next.

acceptedIdeas: The same phase as before
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same phase as before

choices.label: The same phase as before
The opposite phase
A new phase every time

questions.onCorrect: After 29.53 days the Sun–Moon angle has gained a full turn, so the phase repeats.

misconceptions.feedback: The opposite phase comes halfway through the month, after half a turn.
The cycle repeats exactly. Each month brings the same sequence.

questions.prompt: The Moon is 3,475 km across. If it were twice as far as 384,400 km, what would its angular diameter be, in degrees, to two decimal places? Use 1 radian = 57.3°.
hints: Double 384,400 km first.
Divide the diameter by that new distance, then multiply by 57.3.
Round to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: 0.26°. Twice the distance halves the angular size.

misconceptions.feedback: That makes the Moon look larger. Greater distance makes it look smaller.
That is the size at the real distance. Twice as far shrinks it.

questions.prompt: A planet has Earth's mass but twice Earth's radius. By what factor does its surface gravity change compared with Earth's?
hints: Surface gravity is g = GM/r², and M is unchanged.
Doubling r changes g by the inverse square.
Square the 2, then take the reciprocal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: g = GM/r², so doubling r divides g by 2² = 4, a factor of 0.25.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25. With the mass fixed, g falls as 1/r², so doubling the radius divides it by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves g, as if gravity fell in proportion to the distance. It follows the square.
That makes g larger. A larger radius puts the surface farther from the centre, which weakens the pull.

questions.prompt: Which change weakens the gravitational force between two masses?
hints: Look at where r sits in the formula.

acceptedIdeas: Moving them farther apart
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Moving them farther apart

choices.label: Moving them farther apart
Making one of them heavier
Making G larger

questions.onCorrect: Force grows with the masses and falls as r² grows, so more separation weakens it.

misconceptions.feedback: A heavier mass increases the product Mm, which strengthens the pull.
G is a fixed constant. We cannot change it.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the factors?
hints: In F = GMm/r², how are the quantities combined?

acceptedIdeas: Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.

choices.label: Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.
Because the formula adds the masses.
Because force is the sum of two terms.

questions.onCorrect: The force is a product and a quotient, so separate changes multiply together.

misconceptions.feedback: The formula multiplies the masses, it does not add them.
F is built from a product and a quotient, not a sum.

questions.prompt: In g = GM/r², what does M stand for?
hints: Which mass cancelled when we divided by m?

acceptedIdeas: The mass of the body doing the pulling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mass of the body doing the pulling

choices.label: The mass of the body doing the pulling
The mass of the falling object
The mass of the Sun

questions.onCorrect: M belongs to the body whose gravity we are measuring, such as Earth. The falling mass has cancelled.

misconceptions.feedback: The falling mass is m, and it cancelled when we divided by it.
The Sun is just one possible pulling body. M is whichever body's gravity you are measuring.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 4r. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change? Give four decimal places.
hints: Gravity follows an inverse-square law.
Square the factor by which the distance grew.
Take the reciprocal of 4².
questions.onCorrect: 0.0625. Four times the separation divides the force by 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 4. The force follows the inverse square, so the 4 is squared first.
That makes the force grow. It weakens as the bodies move apart.

questions.prompt: Earth’s surface curves away by 5 m over every 8 km, and a ball falls 5 m in its first second. How fast, in km/s, must the ball travel along the ground to keep missing it?
hints: In one second the ball falls 5 m.
The ground must curve away by 5 m in that same second.
How far along the ground does it take for the surface to curve away by 5 m?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ground curves away 5 m over 8 km, and the ball falls 5 m in 1 s, so it must cover 8 km each second: 8 km/s.

questions.onCorrect: 8 km/s. A ball that covers 8 km as it falls 5 m never reaches the ground: it is in orbit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the drop in metres. The speed is how far along the ground the ball must travel in one second.

questions.prompt: A satellite moves slower than the circular speed at its height. What happens?
hints: Gravity pulls it inward faster than its path curves away.

acceptedIdeas: It falls towards the body
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls towards the body

choices.label: It falls towards the body
It escapes
It stays on a circle

questions.onCorrect: Too slow and the pull wins: the path curves into the body instead of round it.

misconceptions.feedback: Escape needs more speed than the circular speed, not less.
A circle needs exactly the circular speed. Slower, the path bends inward.

questions.prompt: Why must r be in metres?
hints: Check the units of GM.

acceptedIdeas: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres too.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres too.

choices.label: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres too.
Metres are the biggest unit.
Square roots only work on metres.

questions.onCorrect: The formula works in SI units. GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres for the answer to be in m/s.

misconceptions.feedback: Metres are not the biggest unit. The reason is the units of GM.
A square root works on any positive number. The units of GM are what matter.

questions.prompt: A probe moves at exactly the escape speed. What happens to it?
hints: The path opens out rather than closing.

acceptedIdeas: It never returns
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It never returns

choices.label: It never returns
It circles at a fixed height
It falls back

questions.onCorrect: At the escape speed the path just fails to close, so the probe never returns.

misconceptions.feedback: A circle needs the smaller circular speed.
Falling back needs a speed below the circular speed.

questions.prompt: A satellite circles Earth at r = 8,000 km from Earth's centre. Find its speed in km/s, to two decimal places. GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s².
hints: Use v = √(GM/r) with r in metres.
Divide GM by 8 × 10⁶ m.
Take the square root and convert from m/s to km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 7.06 km/s. Circular speed falls as r grows: higher satellites move slower.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the escape speed at this distance. The circular speed has no 2 under the root.
That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 for km/s.

questions.prompt: The noon Sun’s overhead point moves from the Tropic of Cancer, 23.4° N, to the Tropic of Capricorn, 23.4° S. Through how many degrees of latitude does it travel?
hints: Where is the Sun overhead in June, and where in December?
The two tropics lie on opposite sides of the equator.
Add the two distances from the equator.
questions.onCorrect: 46.8°. The overhead point crosses the equator, travelling twice the tilt.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance from the equator to one tropic. The spot has to cross the equator to reach the other.

questions.prompt: What is the Sun's declination around 21 December?
hints: In December the northern hemisphere leans away from the Sun.
questions.onCorrect: −23.4°. The Sun is south of the celestial equator by the tilt in December.

misconceptions.feedback: That is June. In December the northern hemisphere leans away, so the Sun is south of the equator.
0° happens at the equinoxes in March and September, not at a solstice.

questions.prompt: Why is the Sun's declination +23.4° in June?
hints: Think about which way the tilted axis points.

acceptedIdeas: The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.

choices.label: The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.
Earth is closest to the Sun then.
The Sun moves north through space.

questions.onCorrect: The axis keeps its direction while Earth orbits, so in June the north leans towards the Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: Distance does not set the declination. Earth is nearest the Sun in January.
The Sun is not moving. Earth's tilted axis makes it appear to shift north and south.

questions.prompt: Which Sun spreads the same beam of sunlight over more ground?
hints: Picture a torch shone straight down, then at a slant.

acceptedIdeas: The Sun 20° above the horizon
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Sun 20° above the horizon

choices.label: The Sun 20° above the horizon
The Sun 60° above the horizon
Both spread it equally

questions.onCorrect: A lower Sun spreads its beam thinner. The ground gets less energy per square metre.

misconceptions.feedback: A higher Sun is nearer to overhead and spreads its beam least.
A beam covers 1/sin h times the ground, which changes with the altitude h.

questions.prompt: Sydney lies at 33.9° S, so φ = −33.9°. Find the noon Sun's altitude there at the June solstice, in degrees, to one decimal place.
hints: Southern latitudes take a minus sign, and so does the subtraction that follows.
Work out −33.9 − 23.4 and ignore its sign.
Subtract that size from 90.
questions.onCorrect: 32.7°. Sydney is in the south, so the June Sun is far from its latitude and sits low.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. Take it away from 90°.
That is Sydney's December figure. In June the Sun is north of the equator, away from Sydney.

questions.prompt: Star X has 3 times the fuel of star Y and burns it 12 times as fast. How long does X's fuel last compared with Y's? Give a decimal.
hints: Lasting time is fuel divided by burn rate.
Take Y's fuel and rate as 1, so X's are 3 and 12.
Divide 3 by 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lifetime = fuel ÷ burn rate = 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 of Y's.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25. X has more fuel, but it burns so much faster that the fuel lasts a quarter as long.

misconceptions.feedback: That is upside down. More fuel lengthens the life and a faster burn shortens it.
That multiplies fuel and rate. Fuel lengthens the time and burn rate shortens it, so divide.

questions.prompt: A star has more mass than the Sun. How does its main-sequence life compare?
hints: Compare how fast fuel and burn rate grow with mass.

acceptedIdeas: Shorter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shorter

choices.label: Shorter
Longer
The same

questions.onCorrect: Burn rate grows much faster than fuel, so heavier stars live shorter lives.

misconceptions.feedback: More fuel, yes, but the burn rate grows far faster. The burn rate wins.
Burn rate depends strongly on mass, so lifetimes differ.

questions.prompt: Why is the exponent in M⁻²·⁵ negative?
hints: Divide M by M³·⁵.

acceptedIdeas: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.

choices.label: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.
Lifetimes are always small numbers.
Mass is measured in solar units.

questions.onCorrect: M ÷ M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵: the burn rate outgrows the fuel, so the lifetime shrinks.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign has nothing to do with size. It comes from dividing M by M³·⁵.
Solar units set the scale, not the sign of the exponent.

questions.prompt: Using L ∝ M³·⁵, how many times the Sun's luminosity does a 10 M☉ main-sequence star have? Give the nearest hundred.
hints: Raise the mass ratio to the power 3.5.
Split 10³·⁵ into 10³ × 10⁰·⁵.
Multiply 1,000 by √10, then round to the nearest hundred.
questions.onCorrect: 3,200 L☉. A tenfold mass gives thousands of times the light.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 10 by 3.5. The exponent is a power applied to 10.
That is 10³. The exponent is 3.5, which adds a square root of 10.

questions.prompt: If the sky makes one full turn of 360° in 24 hours, through how many degrees does it turn in one hour?
hints: The turning is steady, so every hour gets an equal share.
Share the 360° equally between the 24 hours.
Work out 360 ÷ 24.
questions.onCorrect: 15°. A steady full turn shared across 24 hours gives 15° every hour.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole circle, turned in a day. The question asks about one hour.
That is the number of hours. The answer is an angle.

questions.prompt: Which describes a celestial pole?
hints: Think about what Earth’s axis points at.

acceptedIdeas: The spot the whole sky seems to turn about
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The spot the whole sky seems to turn about

choices.label: The spot the whole sky seems to turn about
The brightest star in the northern sky
The point straight above your head

questions.onCorrect: A celestial pole is where Earth’s axis points. The stars wheel about it, so it never moves.

misconceptions.feedback: A pole is a point in the sky, not a star. Polaris lies close to the north one, but it is only moderately bright.
Straight overhead is the zenith. The pole is overhead only at the North Pole.

questions.prompt: Why can we multiply 15° by the number of hours?
hints: What would change if the sky sped up?

acceptedIdeas: The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.

choices.label: The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.
Multiplying always gives a bigger answer.
Stars move faster later in the night.

questions.onCorrect: Steady turning means each hour adds the same angle, so the total is rate × hours.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger answer is not the reason. Multiplying works because the rate does not change.
The sky turns at a constant rate. A changing rate would break the multiplication.

questions.prompt: A star has a declination of +90°. Where is it in the sky?
hints: Think about what +90° means for latitude on Earth.

acceptedIdeas: At the north celestial pole
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the north celestial pole

choices.label: At the north celestial pole
On the celestial equator
At the south celestial pole

questions.onCorrect: +90° is the north celestial pole, the point the whole sky turns about, so a star there does not circle at all.

misconceptions.feedback: The celestial equator is at declination 0°. +90° is as far north as the sky goes.
The south celestial pole is at −90°. The plus sign means north of the celestial equator.

questions.prompt: A star has turned through 270° of its daily circle. How many hours is that, at 15° per hour?
hints: How many 15° steps fit into the angle?
Divide, rather than multiply.
Work out 270 ÷ 15.
questions.onCorrect: 18 hours. Time is the angle shared out by the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the angle by the rate. To find a time, share the angle out by the rate.
That adds the rate to the angle. Divide to find how many hours fit.

questions.prompt: A navigator measures Polaris 41° above the horizon. Taking Polaris to be at the north celestial pole, what is the ship’s latitude, in degrees north?
hints: Which angle did the last screen say equals the latitude?
The pole’s altitude equals the observer’s latitude.
The navigator measured the pole’s altitude directly.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pole’s altitude equals the latitude, so the ship is at the latitude the navigator measured.

questions.onCorrect: 41° N. Measure the pole star’s altitude and you have your latitude.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 90° minus the altitude, the angle from Polaris up to the point overhead. The latitude equals the altitude itself.

questions.prompt: From latitude 40° N, what is the smallest declination, in degrees, that makes a star circumpolar?
hints: The star’s lowest point has to stay above the horizon.
The condition was δ > 90° − φ.
Put φ = 40° into the right-hand side.
questions.onCorrect: 50°. From 40° N, every star north of declination +50° stays above the horizon all night.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude itself. The limit is 90° minus the latitude.
Adding gives 130°, which no star reaches. The rule subtracts the latitude from 90°.

questions.prompt: At 15° an hour, how many hours does the sky take to turn through 135°?
hints: How many 15° steps fit into 135°?
Divide the angle by the rate.
Work out 135 ÷ 15.
questions.onCorrect: 9 hours. 135° ÷ 15° per hour = 9 h.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. The time is the angle divided by the rate.

questions.prompt: From latitude 30° N, what is the smallest declination, in degrees, that makes a star circumpolar?
hints: A star is circumpolar when its lowest point stays above the horizon.
The limit is a declination, measured from the celestial equator, that depends on the latitude.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude itself. The limit is 90° minus the latitude.

questions.prompt: On the equator the north celestial pole sits on the horizon. How many stars are circumpolar there?
hints: Where would the lowest point of any star’s circle fall, compared with the horizon?

acceptedIdeas: None
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None

choices.label: About half of them
Only the stars very near the north celestial pole
None

questions.onCorrect: None. At latitude 0° a star would need a declination above 90°, and none has one. Every star rises and sets.

misconceptions.feedback: Half the sky is above the horizon at any moment, but every star still spends part of each day below it.
A star near the pole has a small circle, but that circle is centred on the horizon here, so half of it is below the horizon.

flashcards.front: From latitude 41° N, how many degrees above the horizon is the north celestial pole?
flashcards.back: The pole's altitude equals the latitude: 41°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pole's altitude equals the latitude: 41°.

At latitude 60° N on an equinox, what is the Sun's noon altitude in degrees?
flashcards.back: δ = 0°, so the noon altitude is 90° − 60° = 30°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ = 0°, so the noon altitude is 90° − 60° = 30°.

flashcards.front: What percentage of the Moon's visible disc is lit when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 60°?
flashcards.back: (1 − cos 60°)/2 = (1 − 0.5)/2 = 0.25, a quarter of the disc.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (1 − cos 60°)/2 = (1 − 0.5)/2 = 0.25, a quarter of the disc.

An asteroid has an orbital period of 27 years. Using P² = a³, find its semi-major axis in AU.
An orbit has semi-major axis 5 AU and eccentricity 0.2. Find its aphelion distance in AU.
Two masses are moved from separation r to r/2. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?
flashcards.back: F ∝ 1/r²; halving r multiplies F by 2² = 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ 1/r²; halving r multiplies F by 2² = 4.

flashcards.front: Gravity at Earth's surface is 9.82 m/s². Find the field one Earth radius above the surface, in m/s², to three decimal places.
flashcards.back: One radius above the surface is 2R from the centre, so g falls by 2² = 4: 9.82/4 = 2.455 m/s².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One radius above the surface is 2R from the centre, so g falls by 2² = 4: 9.82/4 = 2.455 m/s².

flashcards.front: Escape speed is how many times the circular orbital speed at the same distance? Give three decimal places.
A satellite circles Earth at r = 42,164 km, where GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². Find its speed in km/s, to two decimal places.
flashcards.back: v = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴ / 4.2164 × 10⁷) = 3,075 m/s, about 3.07 km/s. This is the geostationary orbit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: v = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴ / 4.2164 × 10⁷) = 3,075 m/s, about 3.07 km/s. This is the geostationary orbit.

A galaxy's 500.0 nm line is observed at 503.0 nm. Using c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, find its recession speed in km/s.
A star has three times the Sun's radius and the Sun's surface temperature. Find its luminosity in solar units.
A star has half the Sun's surface temperature and exactly the Sun's luminosity. Find its radius in solar radii.
flashcards.back: 1 = R² × (1/2)⁴ = R²/16, so R² = 16 and R = 4 R☉.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 = R² × (1/2)⁴ = R²/16, so R² = 16 and R = 4 R☉.

With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, find the recession velocity of a galaxy 40 Mpc away, in km/s.
